senses.definition: A job, task or other activity that is pleasant or, by extension, easy or simple.
senses.example: Sure, no problem. It'll be a piece of cake.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see piece,‎ cake.

core.definition: Something very easy to do. Used for a task, test, or activity that needs little effort or skill.

pronunciation.tip: 'Of' is reduced to 'uv' in fast speech, and 'piece' rhymes with 'peace.' The main stress falls on 'cake,' so do not give 'piece' the heavy stress.

nuance.connotation: Positive or light. It shows confidence or ease and is usually said with a smile.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'It's a piece of cake' after finishing something easy, like a quiz or a home repair. It is casual and friendly. A natural reply is 'Nice, I knew you could do it,' or simply 'Lucky you!' Do not use it for serious tasks where the person might feel belittled.

distinctions.note: Both mean easy. 'Easy as pie' is slightly older and folksy, while 'a piece of cake' is more common in modern American speech.
'No big deal' focuses on something not being important. 'A piece of cake' focuses on something being simple to do.

collocations: sounds like a piece of cake
a piece of cake for me
the exam was a piece of cake
easy as a piece of cake

examples.everyday: I just fixed the sink myself, and it was a piece of cake.
examples.professional: Migrating the old reports to the new dashboard was a piece of cake once we had the data mapping.
examples.analytical: To call the proof a piece of cake underestimates the conceptual work hidden in its lemma.

nuance.analogy: Like a slice of cake at a birthday party: something easy and enjoyable to take.
nuance.etymology: The phrase is an early 20th-century American expression, probably from the idea of a simple, pleasant treat. The exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a piece of the cake' or 'pieces of cake'; the idiom is fixed as 'a piece of cake.'
Using it for a task that is actually dangerous or serious, which can sound careless.

a-piece-of-cake.etymology: Attested since 1936, originally in American English.

conversation.text: Don't stress about the driving test. Parallel parking is a piece of cake once you practice.
The data migration was a piece of cake compared to last year's.
"How was the hike?" "A piece of cake. We were back by noon."

senses.definition: Expectancy; a condition when an ownership of real property is undetermined; lapse in succession of ownership of estate, or title.
senses.example: The proceeds of the estate shall be held in abeyance in an escrow account until the minor reaches age twenty-one.

senses.definition: Suspension; temporary suppression; dormant condition.
Expectancy of a noble or armigeral title, its right in existence but its exercise suspended.
senses.example: The broad pennant of a commodore first class has been in abeyance since 1958, together with the rank.

core.definition: A temporary suspension, when something is not currently in effect or being acted upon and waits for a later decision.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, BAY, and the final -ance is a weak syllable that sounds like uns. Learners often say uh-BAY-ance with a full vowel, which sounds too formal.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a pause or hold without judgment, though it can imply that something is stalled.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use in abeyance mostly in business, legal, and formal settings, such as a project being on hold or a rule being suspended. In casual conversation, people would say on hold, on ice, or paused. The phrase is common in news about policies and lawsuits.

distinctions.note: Suspension is a general word for stopping something, while abeyance implies a pause that is expected to end in a later decision.
A moratorium is an official legal pause, while abeyance can apply to any project, rule, or right that is temporarily held.
Hold is informal and common in everyday speech, while abeyance is formal and used in writing or serious discussion.

collocations: the rule is held in abeyance

examples.everyday: The kitchen renovation is in abeyance until the contractor gets back to us about the permit.
examples.professional: The product launch remains in abeyance until legal signs off on the data-sharing agreement.
examples.analytical: During the emergency, several constitutional protections were held in abeyance, which raised questions about how long a temporary measure can remain temporary.

nuance.analogy: Like a pot on the stove turned down to the lowest setting: it is still there and ready, but nothing is cooking right now.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French abeiance, 'expectation,' from abaer, 'to gape at, await.'
common_mistakes: Using at instead of in, as in 'at abeyance'; the standard phrase is in abeyance.
Pronouncing the final -ance with a full vowel, which makes the word sound stiff in American speech.

senses.definition: Absence of willpower or decisiveness, especially as a symptom of mental illness.

core.definition: A medical condition in which a person has very little willpower or trouble making decisions and starting actions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on BOO, the second syllable. The final syllables are weak, so the last 'ia' is a soft 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative and clinical. It describes a symptom and should be used with care, since it can sound judgmental if applied to ordinary laziness.
nuance.usage_note: In American medical and psychological writing, 'abulia' with a single 'o' is more common than 'aboulia'. Americans rarely use the word in casual conversation. For everyday tiredness or lack of motivation, say 'low motivation' or 'no energy'.

distinctions.note: Apathy means a lack of interest or concern; aboulia means a lack of will to act or decide, even when the person may still care.
Lethargy means physical or mental sluggishness; aboulia specifically refers to an impaired ability to start or choose actions.

examples.everyday: After the flu, I had almost no energy, but my doctor said it wasn't aboulia, just a normal recovery.
examples.professional: The wellness program tracks employees who report aboulia-like symptoms, such as difficulty starting tasks, and refers them to a clinician.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that aboulia, as a clinical concept, reveals how philosophers have wrongly treated will as a single, unified power.

nuance.analogy: Aboulia is like a car with a full tank and working engine that will not start, because the spark of decision is missing.
nuance.etymology: From Greek a-, 'without', and boulē, 'will' or 'deliberation'.
common_mistakes: Using 'aboulia' for ordinary laziness; it is a clinical term for impaired will.
Using the spelling 'aboulia' in American medical writing, where 'abulia' is more common.

senses.definition: An absolving of sins from ecclesiastical penalties by an authority.
The forgiveness of sins, in a general sense.
The form of words by which a penitent is absolved.
An absolving, or setting free from guilt, sin, or penalty; forgiveness of an offense.
senses.example: Governments granting absolution to the nation.

core.definition: The formal declaration of forgiveness of sins by a priest or minister; more generally, release from guilt or blame.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on LOO, the third syllable, with secondary stress on 'ab'. The ending is /ʃən/, like 'shun'. Americans normally drop the /j/ glide: 'loo', not 'lyoo'.

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive or relieving: freedom from guilt. It can be neutral in church use or ironic in secular use.
nuance.usage_note: In church contexts it names the declaration of forgiveness, especially in Catholic, Orthodox, and Anglican practice. In everyday American speech, 'seeking absolution' means wanting to be freed from guilt or blame, sometimes jokingly. It is a formal word in ordinary talk.

distinctions.note: Forgiveness is the general word; absolution is a formal declaration, often by an authority, especially in church.
A pardon is a legal or official release from punishment, while absolution concerns guilt or sin.
Acquittal is a court verdict of not guilty; absolution frees someone from guilt that may be real.

examples.everyday: He kept apologizing at dinner, as if he needed my absolution for missing the party.
examples.professional: The manager made a public apology, but he knew it would not bring absolution from the team.
examples.analytical: In sacramental theology, absolution is not merely a wish for forgiveness but an act of the Church in the name of Christ.

nuance.analogy: Like a signed receipt stating the debt is paid.
nuance.etymology: From Latin absolutio, from absolvere, 'to set free, release'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable: say ab-suh-LOO-shun.
Confusing it with 'absolute' in meaning.
Saying 'absolution' for any small apology; it suggests guilt and release.
nuance.biblical_note: The word is not in the RSV text, but the idea appears in Christ's authority to forgive sins. In John 20:22-23 the risen Jesus breathes on the disciples and speaks of forgiving and retaining sins. In Matthew 16:19 and 18:18 he speaks of binding and loosing. The Greek 'aphiemi' means to release or forgive.

traditions.view: Absolution is the priest's act in the sacrament of Penance, given in the person of Christ after confession, contrition, and satisfaction. It is understood to truly forgive sins.

In confession, a priest pronounces a prayer of absolution as a ministry of God's mercy within the Church's healing of the soul. Orthodoxy stresses that Christ himself forgives, and the formula is often prayerful rather than judicial.

Lutherans and Anglicans keep forms of absolution, Lutherans valuing private confession and absolution as proclaiming God's forgiveness. Reformed and Baptist traditions typically reject a priestly sacrament, holding that God forgives directly through Christ, though pastors declare the gospel's assurance.

absolution.etymology: From Middle English *absolucion*, *absolucioun*, from Old French *absolution*, from Latin *absolūtiōnem*, accusative singular of *absolūtiō* (“acquittal”), from *absolvō* (“absolve”).

senses.definition: In an abundant manner; in a sufficient degree; in large measure.
Extremely.

core.definition: In large amounts or to a great degree; more than enough, or very clearly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, -BUN-, and make the last two syllables light: 'dunt-lee.' Do not stress the final syllable or say 'uh-bun-DANT-lee.' The -tly ending is pronounced as 't' followed by 'lee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests generosity or clarity, depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say 'abundantly clear' or 'abundantly obvious,' which are common in speech and writing. Other uses, such as 'abundantly grateful,' sound stiff or formal. In everyday speech people usually say 'a lot' or 'really.'

distinctions.note: 'Very' is the everyday intensifier, while 'abundantly' emphasizes a large quantity or a strong, obvious degree.
'Plentifully' focuses on supply, while 'abundantly' can also describe a clear or obvious degree.
'Richly' suggests a sense of quality or luxury, while 'abundantly' emphasizes quantity.

examples.everyday: The tomatoes grew abundantly this year, so we gave bags to every neighbor on the block.
examples.professional: The vendor has been abundantly clear that the license won't cover contractors.
examples.analytical: Paul writes that God is able to do abundantly more than we ask or think, and that claim shapes his account of grace.

nuance.analogy: Like a river spilling over its banks in spring, so there is more than the land can hold.
nuance.etymology: From abundant plus the adverbial suffix -ly, from Latin abundare 'to overflow.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable (uh-bun-DANT-lee) rather than the second.
Using 'abundantly' as a noun, as in 'the abundantly of food,' when the noun is 'abundance.'
nuance.biblical_note: Ephesians 3:20 speaks of God being able to do far more abundantly than all we ask or think, a central text on God's generosity beyond human expectations. John 10:10 describes the life Jesus gives as abundant, using the same idea of fullness. The adverb stresses how God's gifts exceed what people can measure or request.

senses.definition: Familiar with something through repeated experience; adapted to existing conditions.
senses.example: I am not accustomed to walk(ing) long distances.

senses.definition: Familiar through use; usual; customary.

core.definition: Used to something through repeated experience; familiar with it and not surprised by it. Often followed by 'to'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the final 'ed' is pronounced as a 'd' after the 'm', so the word ends in a single consonant cluster 'md' with no extra vowel. The first vowel is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes familiarity without judgment, although it can suggest comfort or routine.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use accustomed often in writing and speech, with 'to' plus a noun or -ing form ('accustomed to the heat'). In casual talk they might say 'used to' instead. Accustomed also means usual or customary, as in 'her accustomed seat', which sounds slightly formal.

distinctions.note: Used to is common in everyday speech and can also describe past habits. Accustomed to has the sense of being familiar with a current situation.
Customary describes what is normal or traditional for a group, and is less personal than accustomed.

examples.everyday: I'm finally accustomed to the spicy food here, so my friends don't have to order for me anymore.
examples.professional: Our team is accustomed to tight deadlines, so the new schedule should not be a problem.
examples.analytical: Accustomed to scarcity, the community reads any abundance as a sign of divine favor.

nuance.analogy: Being accustomed to something is like a hand that automatically reaches for the light switch in your own kitchen: the movement is familiar and no longer requires thought.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'accustom' with the past participle ending '-ed', from Old French 'acostumer'.
common_mistakes: Using 'accustomed' with 'of' or 'with' instead of 'to', as in 'accustomed of' or 'accustomed with'.
Using 'accustomed' with a verb directly, without 'to' and an -ing form, as in 'accustomed work late'.

core.definition: The daughter of Caleb, given in marriage to Othniel for capturing Kiriath-sepher, who asked her father for springs of water.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AK, and pronounce the ch as sh. The final vowel is a reduced uh, not a long ah.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a biblical woman's name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Achsah the same way in Bible study and church. The name is uncommon, so you may hear it mainly in discussions of Judges or Joshua.

examples.everyday: In our Bible reading, Achsah asked her father for springs of water, and that caught my attention.
examples.professional: In the women's ministry lesson, I'll highlight Achsah's request as an example of a woman who asks boldly for what the family needs.
examples.analytical: Achsah's request for water in Joshua 15 and Judges 1 is read by many scholars as a claim on land and resources within a patrilineal inheritance.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Akhsah, traditionally glossed as anklet; the meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ch as a hard k or as in church.
Stressing the final syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'Akhsah, traditionally glossed 'anklet'. Key passages: Joshua 15:16-19, where Caleb gives Achsah to Othniel and she asks for springs of water, receiving the upper and lower springs; Judges 1:12-15, which repeats the story and places it in the conquest of Debir. Achsah is a rare example of a woman who negotiates for property in the biblical text.

senses.definition: A positive emotion combining wonder and approbation; the regarding of another as being wonderful; a feeling of respect for another's skills or attributes, as one might look on a hero or role model.
senses.example: admiration of a war hero

core.definition: A feeling of respect and approval for someone's qualities, skills, or achievements, often mixed with wonder.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RAY, the second-to-last syllable, and the -tion ending sounds like 'shun'. Keep the middle syllable 'muh' very short and reduced, not 'mah'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It expresses approval and respect, and it can feel warm or slightly formal depending on how it is said.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'admiration' for a sincere, respectful feeling about a person's character or work, such as a boss, a coach, or a writer. In casual talk, people more often say 'I really respect her' or 'I look up to him', so 'admiration' sounds a bit more formal and written. You can reply to a compliment with a simple 'Thanks, I appreciate that' rather than repeating the word.

distinctions.note: Respect is a broader feeling that someone deserves consideration or fair treatment, while admiration is a more emotional response to something impressive they have done or are.
Praise is an act of speaking well of someone, whereas admiration is the inner feeling that may or may not be expressed.
Esteem is a more formal, steady opinion of someone's worth, often used in professional or written contexts.

examples.everyday: Everyone at the barbecue had nothing but admiration for how she raised three kids and still ran a marathon.
examples.professional: The whole team has real admiration for how you handled the server outage without blaming anyone.
examples.analytical: Admiration differs from mere approval because it involves a felt recognition of excellence that moves the admirer toward emulation.

nuance.analogy: Admiration is like a warm light pointed at someone's achievements, drawing your attention and making you want to look closer.
nuance.etymology: From Latin admirari, 'to wonder at', from ad- 'at' plus mirari 'to wonder'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'admiration for doing' with the wrong structure; the usual pattern is 'admiration for her courage' or 'admiration of his work', with 'for' or 'of' depending on context.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'AD-mi-ration'; the main stress belongs on RAY.

admiration.etymology: From Middle English *admiracion*, borrowed from Middle French *admiration*, or directly from Latin *admīrātiō*, from prefix *ad-* (“to, towards”) + *mīrō* (“to look at”) + *-ātiō*.

senses.definition: Lewdness or unchastity of thought as well as act, as forbidden by the sixth/seventh commandment; sinful sexual behavior as a category.
senses.example: Thou shalt not commit adultery.

senses.definition: Faithlessness in religion.
The intrusion of a person into a bishopric during the life of the bishop.
Sexual intercourse by a married person with someone other than their spouse. See more synonyms at Thesaurus:cuckoldry.
senses.example: She engaged in adultery because her spouse has a low libido, while hers is very high.

senses.definition: Adulteration; corruption.

core.definition: Voluntary sexual relations between a married person and someone who is not their spouse; in Scripture, also unfaithfulness to God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on DUL, the second syllable. The first syllable is a weak schwa, and the 'u' is as in 'cut'. Do not say 'adult-ery' with stress on 'adult'. Say the last two syllables lightly: /təri/.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative: betrayal, moral failure, and breach of trust. It is also a legal term in some states.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'adultery' in religious, legal, and formal talk. In casual speech they say 'cheating' or 'having an affair'. It sounds serious and judgmental, so it is not a casual word.

distinctions.note: An affair is the everyday word for an adulterous relationship and does not carry the moral weight of adultery.
Infidelity is a broader, more neutral word for unfaithfulness, usually sexual, in a committed relationship.
Fornication means sex between unmarried people, whereas adultery involves at least one married person.
Cheating is the casual word for adultery and is also used for unmarried partners.

examples.everyday: My grandmother said the old movie was scandalous because the plot centered on adultery.
examples.professional: The counselor explained that, although adultery is not a crime in many states, it can matter in a divorce.
examples.analytical: The prophets often describe Israel's idolatry as adultery, using marriage as the central image of the covenant.

nuance.analogy: Like breaking a promise that was meant to be exclusive, in the closest relationship one has.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adulterium, from adulterare, 'to corrupt, defile', ultimately from ad- + alterare 'to alter'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable: say uh-DUL-tuh-ree.
Confusing 'adultery' with 'adult' or 'adulthood'.
Using it for casual unfaithfulness in casual speech where 'cheating' is natural.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'na'aph' and Greek 'moicheia' mean adultery, and the prophets use it as a figure for idolatry. The seventh commandment in the RSV numbering (Exodus 20:14) forbids it. In Matthew 5:27-28 Jesus extends the prohibition to lustful looking. In John 8:1-11 he shows mercy to a woman caught in adultery and tells her to sin no more. Hosea 1-3 uses the prophet's marriage to describe Israel's unfaithfulness and God's steadfast love.

traditions.view: Adultery is a grave sin against the sixth commandment under the Catholic numbering and against the sacrament of marriage; it does not by itself dissolve the marriage bond.
Adultery is a serious sin that breaks the marital union. The Church may allow remarriage after divorce as pastoral mercy, with penance, though it is not the ideal.

Protestants generally count adultery as a sin against the seventh commandment. Many, following Matthew 19:9, allow divorce on grounds of adultery, though some groups discourage divorce and stress forgiveness and reconciliation.

adultery.etymology: With change of suffix, from the Old French *adultere* (“violation of conjugal faith”) (in Bernard of Clairvaux, Sermons, 12c.), a learnèd borrowing from Latin *adulterium*, from *adulterō*.

senses.definition: The state of adverse conditions; state of misfortune or calamity.
An event that is adverse; calamity.

core.definition: Difficult circumstances or bad luck that cause hardship, suffering or struggle over a period of time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on vur, the second syllable, and the final ty is a clear ee sound in American speech. Learners often stress the first syllable or pronounce the final syllable as a full ty.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes hardship, though admiring stories often use it to describe resilience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adversity in speeches, books, essays and sermons, often in phrases such as 'overcome adversity'. In daily talk, people say a hard time or a rough patch. Mentioning adversity can sound dramatic in casual conversation, so use it for serious situations. A natural reply is 'That sounds really tough.'

distinctions.note: Hardship describes a specific difficulty, such as money problems, while adversity is broader and often includes the struggle to overcome many difficulties.
Misfortune refers to bad luck or a single unlucky event, while adversity describes a sustained challenge.

examples.everyday: She's been through a lot of adversity, but she still keeps her sense of humor.
examples.professional: Despite budget cuts and constant adversity, the team shipped the release on time.
examples.analytical: Paul argues in Romans 5 that suffering produces endurance, treating adversity as formative rather than merely destructive.

nuance.analogy: Like a rough sea that tests a ship's hull, adversity reveals what a person or team is made of.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adversitas, opposition or hardship, from adversus, turned against.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'AD-ver-si-tee', which shifts the rhythm.
Confusing adversity with adversary, which is a person or group, not a hardship.
Using adversity for a single small problem, which sounds exaggerated.

adversity.etymology: From Old French *adversité*, from Latin *adversitātem*, the accusative singular of *adversitās*, from *adversus*, the perfect passive participle of *advertō* (“to turn toward”).

senses.definition: The state or quality of being affable, friendly, or approachable.

core.definition: The quality of being warm, friendly and easy to talk to, which makes other people feel comfortable around you.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BIL, and the middle vowels are weak uh sounds. The final -ity is usually ih-tee, and the t is often flapped so it sounds close to a d.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a pleasant, approachable personality and is a compliment, though a somewhat formal one.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use affability in casual talk; they more often say someone is friendly or easygoing. You are more likely to hear it in a job reference, a review, or a description of a politician or host. It is a real compliment but sounds a bit stiff in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Friendliness is the everyday word for warmth; affability adds a relaxed, easygoing quality and sounds more formal.
Charm is an attractive quality that can be deliberate and win people over; affability is a steady, warm disposition.

examples.everyday: The new neighbor has real affability; she waved and asked about my dog within a minute.
examples.professional: Her affability made her the natural choice to host client calls, since people relaxed as soon as she started talking.
examples.analytical: Aristotle treats friendliness in social life as a mean between obsequiousness and surliness, and affability fits that middle ground.

nuance.analogy: Affability is like a warm porch light: it makes people feel welcome before anyone says a word.
nuance.etymology: From Latin affabilis, easy to address, from affari, to speak to, from ad plus fari, to speak.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable with a full ab sound as in cab, instead of a weak uh.
Using the adjective affable when you need the noun affability.

senses.definition: A semitransparent, uncrystallized silicate mineral and semiprecious stone, presenting various tints in the same specimen, with colors delicately arranged and often curved in parallel alternating dark and light stripes or bands, or blended in clouds; various authorities call it a variety of chalcedony, a variety of quartz, or a combination of the two.
One fourteenth of an inch.
A tool used by gold-wire drawers, bookbinders, etc.—so called from the agate fixed in it for burnishing.
A marble made from agate.
A testicle.
The size of type between pearl and nonpareil, standardized as 5+⁄2-point.

core.definition: A hard, banded variety of quartz, often colored in layers, used as a gemstone or polished decorative stone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the first vowel as in 'cat.' The second syllable is a reduced 'ih,' so the word has two syllables, not 'uh-GATE.'

nuance.connotation: neutral: it names a stone, usually in jewelry, geology or collecting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use agate mainly for jewelry, polished stones, rock collecting and marbles. The word is also used in newspaper and advertising design for a very small unit of type, about one fourteenth of an inch, but most people do not know that sense. In Scripture, the term refers to a precious stone in the high priest's breastpiece and in city walls.

distinctions.note: Onyx is a banded chalcedony with straight, parallel bands, while agate usually has curved or cloud-like bands.
Jasper is opaque and colorful, while agate is translucent to semitranslucent.
Chalcedony is the wider family of microcrystalline quartz, and agate is one banded type within it.

examples.everyday: I found a striped agate on the beach, and my daughter wants to make it into a necklace.
examples.professional: The jewelry supplier's catalog lists the agate pendants separately from the quartz stones, because the cutting and polishing costs differ.
examples.analytical: Geologists classify agate as a microcrystalline form of quartz, and its banding reflects successive layers of silica deposited in a cavity.

nuance.analogy: Agate is like a layered cake of quartz, with bands of color stacked and curved inside a stone.
nuance.etymology: From the Latin achates, from the Greek achatēs, the name of a stone, probably from a river in Sicily.
common_mistakes: Saying 'uh-GATE' with the stress on the second syllable and a long A, which sounds like a different word.
Confusing agate with agape, which is a religious term for self-giving love.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word shebo (שְׁבוֹ) appears in the description of the high priest's breastpiece in Exodus 28:19 and 39:12 (RSV), where RSV renders it as agate. Isaiah 54:12 (RSV) describes God making the pinnacles of Jerusalem out of agate, a sign of restoration and beauty. Revelation 21:19-20 (RSV) lists agate among the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem, where it is the second... actually the foundation stones are named in order, and agate is one of them. Ezekiel 27:16 (RSV) lists agate among the wares that Edom traded in Tire.

agate.etymology: From Middle French *agathe*, from Latin *achatēs*, from Ancient Greek *ἀχάτης* (“agate”).

senses.definition: The act of alleviating; relief or mitigation.
The act of reducing pain or anything else unpleasant; easement.

core.definition: The act of making pain, suffering or a problem less severe; the relief that this brings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the AY syllable right before -shun, and give the first syllable light secondary stress. Don't use a hard a in the first syllable, as in ah-leh-vee-AY-shun.

nuance.connotation: Positive, since it refers to relief; in policy and charity contexts it is neutral and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use alleviation in policy, medical and charitable contexts, as in poverty alleviation or pain alleviation. In everyday speech they would say relief or help. It is formal and works well in reports and grant proposals. A natural reply to good news is That's a relief.

distinctions.note: Relief is common and everyday; alleviation is the formal noun for the act of easing something, often in policy or medicine.
Mitigation means reducing harm, often for risks like floods or emissions; alleviation focuses on easing suffering or pressure.
Remission means disease symptoms disappear temporarily; alleviation means symptoms are reduced without necessarily ending.

examples.everyday: The new knee brace brought me a lot of alleviation after the surgery.
examples.professional: Our roadmap includes alleviation of the backlog by adding two QA engineers next quarter.
examples.analytical: Many utilitarian arguments treat the alleviation of suffering as the central moral duty.

nuance.analogy: Like opening a window in a stuffy room: the room is the same, but the air feels easier.
nuance.etymology: From Latin alleviatio, from alleviare 'to lighten', from ad 'to' and levis 'light'.
common_mistakes: Using alleviation as a verb; the verb is alleviate
Stressing the second syllable (LEE) instead of the AY before -shun

senses.definition: A formal speech, especially one which is regarded as authoritative and forceful.

The question put to a convicted defendant by a judge after the rendering of the verdict in a trial, in which the defendant is asked whether he or she wishes to make a statement to the court before sentencing; the statement made by a defendant in response to such a question; the legal right of a defendant to make such a statement.

The legal right of a victim, in some jurisdictions, to make a statement to a court prior to sentencing of a defendant convicted of a crime causing injury to that victim; the actual statement made to a court by a victim.
A pronouncement by a pope to an assembly of church officials concerning a matter of church policy.
The mode of information dissemination in which media broadcasts are transmitted to multiple receivers with no or very limited capability of a two-way exchange of information.

core.definition: A formal, authoritative speech; in US law, a defendant's statement to the court before sentencing.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KYOO, the third syllable. Learners often stress the first syllable or confuse it with 'allocation'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in legal use and solemn in formal speeches. It sounds stiff in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear allocution in courtroom news, where a judge asks a defendant whether they wish to speak before sentencing. The right of allocution is protected in many American courts. In ordinary speech it sounds very formal, and people would say 'speech' or 'address' instead.

distinctions.note: Allocation means distributing resources, while allocution means a formal address, especially a statement to a court.
An oration is any formal public speech, while allocution specifically refers to an authoritative address or a defendant's statement before sentencing.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's trial ended, and the judge gave him a chance to speak before sentencing, but he decided not to make an allocution.
examples.professional: Our legal team reviewed the transcript and confirmed that the defendant's allocution was taken before the sentence was entered.
examples.analytical: As a moment when the defendant addresses the court, allocution raises questions about remorse and the purpose of punishment.

nuance.analogy: Like the last word a defendant gets before the verdict's consequences are announced.
nuance.etymology: From Latin allocutio, 'address', from alloqui, 'to speak to', from ad, 'to', plus loqui, 'to speak'.
common_mistakes: Confusing allocution with allocation, which is about distributing resources.
Using allocution for any speech; it usually refers to a formal address or a court statement.

senses.definition: The spiritual or mystical interpretation of a word or passage beyond the literal, allegorical or moral sense (especially in Biblical criticism).

core.definition: The spiritual or mystical interpretation of a text or passage, looking beyond its literal and moral meaning toward heavenly or ultimate truth.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable, AN, and the final syllable is 'jee', not 'juh' or 'gee'. The middle 'uh' is reduced, and the g in the middle is hard.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in theological discussion. It names a careful reading method and carries no negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans in seminaries, Bible study groups, and theology courses use anagoge when discussing the medieval fourfold method of reading scripture. In ordinary conversation, people would say 'spiritual meaning' or 'heavenly meaning'. Use it in an academic or theological setting, and be ready to explain it, because many listeners will not know the term.

distinctions.note: Allegory is a symbolic reading in which events stand for other things, often doctrinal, while anagoge specifically points to heavenly or eschatological meaning.
Tropology is the moral sense of a text, teaching how to live, while anagoge concerns the final destiny and heavenly reality.

collocations: the anagogic meaning of the text

examples.everyday: My roommate read the old story as being about heaven, an anagogic reading I'd never thought of before.
examples.professional: In the Sunday school curriculum, we explain the anagogic sense so teachers don't reduce every story to a simple moral.
examples.analytical: Medieval exegetes, following Aquinas, distinguished the anagogic sense, which points to eternal life, from the moral sense that teaches right conduct.

nuance.analogy: Like a map that shows not only the roads you are on, but the destination above them.
nuance.etymology: From Late Greek anagōgē, 'a leading up', from ana- 'up' plus agein 'to lead'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'gee' instead of 'jee'.
Confusing anagoge with anachronism, which is a word about time.
Using anagoge for any spiritual feeling, when it refers to a method of interpreting a text.

senses.definition: Placing humans at the center of something, giving preference to humans above all other considerations.

core.definition: Placing human beings at the center of thought, judgment or value, so that human interests are treated as more important than all others.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SEN, and the earlier syllables are reduced, so 'anthro' sounds like 'an-thruh' and 'pocentric' sounds like 'puh-SEN-trik'. The 'th' is voiceless, as in 'thin'.

nuance.connotation: Often negative or critical in environmental ethics, where it describes a view that ignores nonhuman life. In theology or philosophy it can be neutral, meaning simply human-centered.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in academic, philosophical, environmental and theological writing, and in debates about nature and ethics. In casual talk, people say 'human-centered' or 'people first' instead. The word is often used to criticize a view, so it may sound like an accusation.

distinctions.note: Anthropocentric means putting humans at the center of value, while anthropomorphic means giving human form or traits to something non-human.
Theocentric puts God at the center of reality and value, and is often used in theology as the contrast to anthropocentric.
Biocentric gives moral value to all living things, not only to humans, so it is a broader alternative to anthropocentric views.

examples.everyday: My neighbor thinks the whole forest should be cut down for houses, which is a very anthropocentric way of seeing things.
examples.professional: The product team kept designing for convenience, but the research showed the approach was too anthropocentric and ignored how the app affected local wildlife.
examples.analytical: Lynn White's critique treats Western Christian thought as anthropocentric, and defenders of the tradition argue that stewardship reflects a God-centered view of creation.

nuance.analogy: An anthropocentric view is like a map where your own house is drawn in the middle and everything else is placed around it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'anthrōpos' (human being) and 'kentron' (center), with the English suffix -ic.
common_mistakes: Confusing anthropocentric with anthropomorphic, which means giving human traits to animals or objects.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'an-throh-puh-SEN-trick', where the 'ick' should be a short 'ik'.

senses.definition: A philosophy that rejects foundationalism.

core.definition: The philosophical view that knowledge, justification or meaning does not rest on fixed, self-evident foundations, but on other beliefs, practices or social agreement.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on DAY in 'foundation', and the word 'anti' is usually said as 'AN-tee'. Reduce the middle syllables of 'foundational' so they sound like 'fown-DAY-shuh-nul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy, where it names a position. It can sound controversial in debates about truth and religion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in philosophy, epistemology, theology and literary theory, usually when discussing Descartes, pragmatism or the work of Richard Rorty. It is rarely used in everyday conversation. A casual speaker would say 'nobody can be certain of everything', and the term is a technical way of naming that view.

distinctions.note: Anti-foundationalism rejects self-evident foundations but does not always deny objective truth, while relativism holds that truth is relative to a culture or perspective.
Coherentism holds that beliefs are justified by their mutual support in a web, which is one anti-foundationalist position, though anti-foundationalism is broader.
Foundationalism is the view that beliefs must rest on basic, self-evident beliefs, and anti-foundationalism is its direct opponent.

examples.everyday: My brother-in-law says nobody can really prove anything, and I told him that's a kind of anti-foundationalism, which made him laugh.
examples.professional: In our analytics meeting, the anti-foundationalism debate matters less than whether the model predicts customer churn accurately.
examples.analytical: Anti-foundationalism denies that beliefs must rest on self-evident basic truths, a claim that Descartes' project was designed to answer.

nuance.analogy: Anti-foundationalism is like a house built on a web of beams that support each other, rather than on a single stone at the bottom.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'anti' (against) and English 'foundationalism', from Latin 'fundare' (to lay a foundation).
common_mistakes: Omitting the hyphen, or writing 'antifoundationalism' inconsistently in academic writing.
Confusing anti-foundationalism with relativism, which is a stronger and different claim.

senses.definition: Pertaining to apostles or their practice or teaching; pertaining to the apostles (of early Christianity) or their teachings.
senses.example: an apostolic mission

senses.definition: According to the doctrines of the apostles; delivered or taught by the apostles.
senses.example: apostolic faith or practice

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the pope or the papacy; papal.
Of or pertaining to the Catholic missions.
A member of the Apostolici.

core.definition: Relating to the apostles of early Christianity, or to the teaching or authority they passed down, or to the Pope as successor of Peter.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STAH, the third syllable, with a short 'ih' in the final syllable. Keep the middle 'uh' reduced, and don't stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in religious contexts. In everyday talk, it can sound grand or mildly ironic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use apostolic mainly in religious, theological and historical writing. Churches use it in names like Apostolic Church or Apostolic Fathers. Outside of religion, it sounds lofty, so describing a boss's zeal as apostolic would sound playful or overblown.

distinctions.note: Apostolical is an older and less common form; apostolic is the standard form in American usage.
Papal refers specifically to the Pope; apostolic can refer to the apostles, to early church teaching, or to the Pope as apostolic successor.

examples.everyday: My friend's church claims an apostolic heritage that goes back to the first century.
examples.professional: The consultant spoke with an almost apostolic zeal about the new process, which made the team uneasy.
examples.analytical: For Irenaeus, apostolic teaching is the standard against which later doctrines must be measured.

nuance.analogy: Like an original recipe that has been handed down through generations, where each cook claims to follow the first chef's exact steps.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin apostolicus, from Greek apostolikos, relating to an apostle.
common_mistakes: Confusing apostolic with apostolical, which is less common in American usage.
Stressing the first syllable, as in AP-uh-stahl-ik.
Using apostolic to mean 'papal' in all contexts, when it has broader meanings.
nuance.biblical_note: The adjective is not in the Bible, but it comes from the Greek apostolos. Acts 2:42 describes the believers as devoted to the apostles' teaching, and Ephesians 2:20 says the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets.

senses.definition: The unbroken chain of consecrations by laying on of hands from the Apostles of Jesus Christ to the bishops, and from to bishop to bishop through the ages.

core.definition: The doctrine that bishops today are linked to the original apostles through an unbroken line of ordination, giving continuity of authority and teaching.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on STOL (STAH-lik in many American accents with the cot-caught merger) and on SESH in 'succession.' Do not say 'suk-SEE-shun'; the vowel is short e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a term; it can be positive or contested depending on church tradition.
nuance.usage_note: Used in church history, theology, and discussions among Christians about authority and ministry. It comes up when comparing churches. Say it with care, since churches differ about what it requires.

distinctions.note: Apostolicity is the broader quality of faithfulness to the apostles' teaching; apostolic succession stresses the line of ordained bishops.
Ordination is a single act of setting apart a minister; apostolic succession is the chain of such acts across generations.
Tradition is handed-down teaching or practice generally; apostolic succession is specifically about the transmission of episcopal office.

examples.everyday: My Anglican neighbor told me his church values apostolic succession, so he cares who ordained the bishop.
examples.professional: In the ecumenical dialogue, the delegates compared how each church understands apostolic succession.
examples.analytical: Irenaeus appeals to the lines of bishops in the great sees as evidence that the apostolic teaching has been preserved.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay baton passed hand to hand from the first runner to the present one.
nuance.etymology: Apostolic from Greek apostolos, 'one sent'; succession from Latin successio, 'a following after.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'apostle-ic' instead of ap-uh-STAH-lik.
Assuming all Christians accept it in the same way.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture does not use the phrase. Related ideas include Jesus sending out the Twelve (Matthew 28:19-20), and Paul instructing Timothy to entrust teaching to faithful people who will teach others (2 Timothy 2:2). Also, 1 Timothy 4:14 mentions Timothy's gift received with the laying on of hands by the council of elders.

traditions.view: Bishops stand in an unbroken line from the apostles, and this continuity is tied to the Church's life, faith, and sacraments. Communion in the apostolic faith is essential, not only a lineage of hands.

Bishops are successors of the apostles through valid ordination in communion with the pope, and this ensures the authority to teach and administer the sacraments. Catholic teaching recognizes Orthodox succession as valid.

Views differ. Anglicans and many Lutherans (such as in Sweden) keep the historic episcopate, while Reformed, Baptist, and Pentecostal churches generally stress succession of apostolic teaching rather than of ordination.

senses.definition: Clothing.
Aspect, guise, form.
A small ornamental piece of embroidery worn on albs and some other ecclesiastical vestments.
Furniture of a ship, such as masts, sails, rigging, anchors, guns, etc.
To dress or clothe; to attire.
To furnish with apparatus; to equip; to fit out.
senses.example: ships appareled to fight

senses.definition: To dress with external ornaments; to cover with something ornamental.
senses.example: trees appareled with flowers

core.definition: Clothing, especially clothing of a particular type or style, such as formal wear or sportswear.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PAR, and keep the first syllable reduced. The 'r' is pronounced clearly, and the final syllable is light and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In retail and business it is an ordinary word; in everyday talk, 'clothes' or 'clothing' is more common.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use apparel in stores, the fashion business and formal writing. Retail chains and trade groups use the term often, as in 'men's apparel' or 'the apparel industry.' In casual conversation, most people say 'clothes' or 'clothing.'

distinctions.note: Clothes is the everyday word; apparel is more formal or commercial and often suggests a category of goods.
Attire suggests a particular style of dress, often formal; apparel is broader and more neutral.

examples.everyday: The store has a whole section of formal apparel for weddings.
examples.professional: Our apparel division reported strong sales in the spring quarter.
examples.analytical: The word apparel emphasizes outward dress as a sign of role and rank.

nuance.analogy: Like a label on a box that names the category of goods, rather than describing any single item.
nuance.etymology: From Old French apareillier, 'to prepare, make equal,' from Latin ad- plus par, 'equal.'
common_mistakes: Using apparel in casual speech where clothes would be more natural.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'pa-rel' with a long a rather than the reduced vowel of 'par' used in American speech.
Using apparel as a countable noun, when it is usually uncountable.

senses.definition: The mind's perception of itself as the subject or actor in its own states, unifying past and present experiences; self-consciousness, perception that reflects upon itself.
Psychological or mental perception; recognition.
The general process or a particular act of mental assimilation of new experience into the totality of one's past experience.

core.definition: In philosophy and psychology, the process by which the mind becomes aware of a new experience by relating it to what it already knows.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SEP, the third syllable. The middle 'er' is a quick, rhotic schwa, so do not stress it. Keep the final 'shun' short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a technical term in philosophy and psychology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use apperception mainly in philosophy, psychology and education courses. It is not used in everyday talk. Speakers who need a simpler word would say 'awareness' or 'self-awareness,' depending on context.

distinctions.note: Perception is the general act of noticing through the senses; apperception is the mind's reflective awareness of its own experience and how new things fit into it.
Consciousness is the general state of being aware; apperception specifically describes how new experience is assimilated into prior experience.

examples.everyday: My professor says apperception is why we can notice ourselves thinking.
examples.professional: In the design review, we talked about how the team's apperception of the bug changed after the first test.
examples.analytical: Kant's transcendental apperception is the unity of consciousness that makes it possible for experience to be my experience.

nuance.analogy: Like a librarian who not only shelves a new book but notices how it changes the whole collection.
nuance.etymology: From German Apperzeption, coined in philosophy from French aperception, from Latin ad- plus percipere, 'to perceive.'
common_mistakes: Confusing apperception with perception, which is more general.
Using it casually, when awareness or insight would be more natural.
Misspelling it as 'apperseption.'

apperception.etymology: Borrowed from French *aperception* (, used by Gottfried Leibniz (1646–1716)).

senses.definition: A dance position in which the dancer stands on one leg, with the other raised backwards, and the arms outstretched.
Elaborate or ornate creations in general.
An elaborate design of intertwined floral figures or complex geometrical patterns, mainly used in Islamic art and architecture.
An ornate composition, especially for the piano.
To move in an arabesque motion.
To decorate with an arabesque pattern.

core.definition: A ballet pose balanced on one leg with the other leg extended straight behind and the arms outstretched.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the final syllable, BESK, and the first syllables are light. The final 'k' is a clear, unreleased sound, so do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Positive and elegant. It suggests grace and beauty, whether describing dance or decorative design.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear arabesque in ballet, dance classes, or gymnastics talk, where it names a standing pose. The word also describes an ornate decorative pattern, especially in Islamic art, and in design talk. In a dance class, a teacher might say 'Lift into arabesque'. A natural reply is simply to show the pose or say 'Got it'.

distinctions.note: A pirouette is a spinning turn on one leg. An arabesque is a held pose with one leg extended behind.
Filigree is delicate metalwork or fine ornamental lace-like detail. An arabesque is a flowing decorative pattern with interlaced or curving forms.

examples.everyday: My daughter is learning to hold an arabesque without wobbling at her dance class.
examples.professional: The set designer used an arabesque motif on the lobby walls to give the theater a stylish feel.
examples.analytical: The architect's arabesque reflects a worldview in which infinite pattern signals the unseen order of creation.

nuance.analogy: Like a swan on one leg in a still pond, long and balanced, with the other leg reaching out behind.
nuance.etymology: From Italian arabesco 'in the Arabic style', from Arabo 'Arab'.
common_mistakes: Putting stress on the first syllable (AR-uh-besk) instead of the final syllable.
Using arabesque as a general word for anything ornate, rather than a specific pattern or pose.
Confusing it with arabic, the adjective for the language or people.

core.definition: A mountainous region in eastern Anatolia where Noah's ark came to rest after the flood; today Mount Ararat in eastern Turkey.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, the second syllable is a reduced schwa, and the last syllable rhymes with 'cat'. Avoid AH-ruh-rot, which mispronounces the vowels.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it is a place name with religious and national significance for Christians and Armenians.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Mount Ararat for the snowcapped peak on the border of Turkey, Armenia and Iran. The Bible uses the plural mountains of Ararat for a region, so it is more accurate to say Ararat in a biblical context. Americans may see Ararat on brandy bottles or Armenian restaurant menus.

distinctions.note: The Bible names the mountains of Ararat as a region, while Mount Ararat is the modern name of a specific peak.

examples.everyday: Did you know Mount Ararat is in Turkey, even though it's sacred to Armenians?
examples.professional: Our Yerevan office has a view of Mount Ararat, and the client loved the photo we sent.
examples.analytical: Genesis 8:4 places the ark on the mountains of Ararat, a reading that shapes how interpreters locate the flood narrative in real geography.

nuance.analogy: Like a landmark on a map that everyone recognizes, Ararat is the mountain that anchors the flood story.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Ararat, the biblical equivalent of Assyrian Urartu, the kingdom of Urartu.
common_mistakes: Misspelling the name as Arrarat with an extra r.
Pronouncing the first syllable as AH instead of AIR.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name is 'Ararat (אררט), used for a region of mountains in eastern Anatolia. Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat after the flood. 2 Kings 19:37 records that the sons of Sennacherib escaped to the land of Ararat. Jeremiah 51:27 calls for the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni and Ashkenaz to be summoned against Babylon.

senses.definition: In an arduous manner.
senses.example: perform arduously

core.definition: In a way that is very difficult and demanding, requiring great effort and endurance over time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the middle syllables are quick and light, so it sounds like AHR-joo-us-lee. Do not add an extra syllable in the -ous part, and keep the r strong at the start.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing determined effort; it highlights hard work done steadily over time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use arduously in formal writing, history books, news, and speeches about long struggles, as in arduously researched or arduously earned. In casual talk, people say hard, with a lot of effort, or the hard way. Using it to describe a simple chore may sound overly formal.

distinctions.note: Hard is the everyday word and is far more common in speech; arduously sounds written and emphasizes long, tiring effort.
Diligently stresses careful, steady work and attention; arduously stresses exhaustion and difficulty.

examples.everyday: She trained arduously for the marathon all winter, running in the cold before work.
examples.professional: The team arduously rebuilt the search index after the outage, working late for two weeks.
examples.analytical: The historian's argument is arduously researched, drawing on archival letters that earlier scholars never reached.

nuance.analogy: Like pushing a heavy cart uphill one step at a time.
nuance.etymology: From arduous plus the adverbial suffix -ly, from Latin arduus, steep or difficult.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in ar-DOO-us-lee.
Using arduously in casual speech, where hard or with a lot of effort sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A prefix appended to a telephone number indicating the geographical area.

core.definition: The three-digit number at the start of a US or Canadian phone number that identifies the geographic region where the line is located.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable of 'area' is AIR, not 'uh-REE,' and the main stress falls on KODE in 'code.' Most Americans say the 'ea' like 'air' and reduce the final syllable to 'uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it has no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'area code' when giving a phone number, such as 'It's a 415 area code.' Since most of the US requires ten-digit dialing, you must dial the area code even for local calls. People often say 'the 312 area code' to mean Chicago, although mobile numbers no longer reliably show location.

distinctions.note: A country code, such as 1 for the US or 44 for the UK, identifies a whole country; an area code narrows it to a region within the country.
A ZIP code is a five-digit postal code for mail delivery and is not used for dialing phone numbers.

examples.everyday: My sister still has a 503 area code, even though she moved to Texas years ago.
examples.professional: Please include the area code in the dial-in number you send to the client.
examples.analytical: Area codes index geography, but number portability means they no longer reliably track where a caller lives.

nuance.analogy: Like a town name on a postal address: it points you to the region before you reach the exact house.
nuance.etymology: 'Area' comes from Latin 'area,' meaning an open level space; 'code' comes from Latin 'codex,' meaning a book or system of rules.
common_mistakes: Leaving off the area code for local calls, which often fails in the US today
Stressing the second syllable of 'area' instead of saying AIR-ee-uh

conversation.text: What's the area code for Chicago?
I didn't recognize the area code, so I let it go to voicemail.
You need to dial the area code, even for local calls here.

senses.definition: Of or relating to argumentation; specifically, presenting a logical argument or line of reasoning; argumentive, discursive.
Prone to argue or dispute.

core.definition: Inclined to argue or dispute constantly; quarrelsome. Used of people, tones, and writing that seems combative.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MEN, with a lighter stress on ahr, and the unstressed syllables reduce to uh. Non-native speakers often stress the noun ARgyoo-ment, but argumentative moves the stress to the -MEN- syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes someone who argues too much or looks for conflict, though the word can be neutral in logic when it means 'reasoned' (an argumentative essay).
nuance.usage_note: Americans use argumentative mostly to criticize a person's attitude, as in 'Why are you being so argumentative today?' It is common in everyday speech, and a natural reply is 'Sorry, I didn't mean to pick a fight.' In academic writing, an argumentative essay simply means one that takes a clear position and defends it.

distinctions.note: Contentious is more formal and describes someone who likes to fight or a topic that provokes conflict; argumentative is more everyday and focuses on the habit of arguing.
Quarrelsome implies actual fights and bickering, while argumentative can describe someone who just loves to debate and disagree.

examples.everyday: Don't get so argumentative with the waiter. He's just trying to help you pick a wine.
examples.professional: Her email was so argumentative that the client read it as an attack instead of a proposal, so let's rewrite it.
examples.analytical: The essay is argumentative in structure, but its central premise is never defended, so the conclusion does not follow.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who keeps blowing the whistle on every play, the argumentative person can't let a point pass without contesting it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin argumentum, from arguere, meaning to make clear, prove, or accuse.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in the noun ARgument, instead of the -MEN- syllable.
Using argumentative to mean 'having a good argument' in everyday speech; it usually suggests a negative attitude.

argumentative.etymology: From Late Middle English *argumentatif* (“syllogistic, sophistic”), from Old French *argumentatif*, *argumentative* and Medieval Latin, Late Latin *argūmentātīvus*, from Latin *argūmentātor* + *-īvus*.

senses.definition: The feeling or experience of being astonished; great surprise.
senses.example: The class looked on in astonishment as their teacher proceeded to tear the pages out of the textbook.

senses.definition: Something very surprising.

core.definition: A feeling of great surprise, often mixed with wonder; or something that causes this feeling.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on STAH, the second syllable. The final -ment is unstressed and reduced to a quick 'muhnt' with a schwa, not a full 'mint' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, showing wonder. It can also be negative when the surprise is shocking or unwelcome.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use astonishment mainly in phrases like 'to my astonishment' or 'in astonishment,' and it appears in both speech and writing. It sounds a bit more formal than 'surprise,' so in casual talk people often say 'I was so surprised.' It works well in storytelling.

distinctions.note: Surprise is the everyday word for the feeling of the unexpected; astonishment is stronger and more intense.
Amazement usually suggests admiring wonder; astonishment can include shock or disbelief.
Shock is sudden and often unpleasant; astonishment can be pleasant, awed, or mixed.

examples.everyday: To my astonishment, the restaurant had a free table on a Saturday night.
examples.professional: To everyone's astonishment, the pilot ran for a full week without a single failure.
examples.analytical: Many readers meet the parables with astonishment before they reach any explanation, and that first reaction matters for interpretation.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden drop in an elevator: the body feels it before the mind can explain it.
nuance.etymology: From astonish plus the suffix -ment, meaning 'the state or result of astonishing'.
common_mistakes: Using the noun 'astonishment' where the adjective 'astonishing' is needed, as in 'It was a astonishment' instead of 'It was astonishing.'
Writing 'astonishment of' when the usual phrase is 'astonishment at' something or 'to my astonishment'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind astonishment is often ekstasis, which literally means 'standing outside oneself' and can describe amazement, trance, or ecstasy. Mark 5:42 describes the onlookers overcome with amazement when Jesus raised Jairus' daughter. Acts 3:10 describes people filled with wonder and astonishment at the healing of the lame man at the Temple gate.

senses.definition: The state of being asynchronous, or out of synchronization.

core.definition: The state of not happening at the same time or not being in step; a lack of synchronization between events, processes or signals.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SING, as in asynchronous, and the final y is a long ee. Learners often stress the last syllable, saying ay-sing-kruh-NEE.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in discussions of people it can suggest a mismatch or lack of harmony.
nuance.usage_note: Mostly used in computing, electronics, neuroscience and biology, and occasionally about schedules or relationships. Americans more often use the adjective asynchronous. In everyday talk, out of sync is the natural phrase.

distinctions.note: Asynchronous is the adjective; asynchrony is the abstract state, so say the asynchrony between clocks, not the asynchronous between clocks.
Out of sync is casual everyday language; asynchrony is technical and precise.

examples.everyday: The video and audio are out of sync, so there's a bit of asynchrony in the stream.
examples.professional: The dashboard shows asynchrony between the sensor data and the database timestamps, so we need to fix the clock sync.
examples.analytical: Asynchrony in neural signals raises the question of whether timing alone can carry meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a choir where each singer starts a beat late, so the harmony falls apart.
nuance.etymology: From asynchronous, from Greek a- 'not' plus synchronos 'at the same time'.
common_mistakes: Using asynchrony as an adjective instead of asynchronous.
Stressing the final syllable, as in ay-sing-kruh-NEE.

senses.definition: A form of neural network designed to learn codings.

core.definition: A neural network trained to compress input data into a compact code and then reconstruct the original input.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KOH in encoder: aw-toh-in-KOH-der. The in in the middle is a reduced vowel, and the final -er is a weak, r-colored sound, not a full 'ur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term used in machine learning and data science.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and machine learning engineers use autoencoder in technical discussions, papers and meetings. It is usually written as one word, although some writers hyphenate it as auto-encoder. In casual conversation, people describe what it does rather than name it.

distinctions.note: A variational autoencoder learns a probability distribution over the latent code, which makes generating new samples more principled.
PCA is a linear method for reducing dimensions, while autoencoders can learn nonlinear compressions.

examples.everyday: My coworker used an autoencoder to clean up noisy audio files, and I still don't fully understand how it works.
examples.professional: We trained an autoencoder on normal transactions, so unusual payments show a high reconstruction error.
examples.analytical: The bottleneck in an autoencoder forces the network to learn a compressed representation that keeps only the features needed to rebuild the input.

nuance.analogy: An autoencoder is like summarizing a book in a few sentences and then trying to rewrite the whole book from that summary.
nuance.etymology: Combines auto- 'self' with encoder, a device that converts input into code, because it reproduces its own input.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing encoder as EN-coder; the stress is en-KOH-der.
Confusing autoencoders with autoregressive models, which predict the next value in a sequence.

conversation.text: An autoencoder learns to compress the input and then reconstruct it from the compressed code.
We flag transactions that the autoencoder reconstructs poorly as possible anomalies.

senses.definition: A building, often found on a farm, used for storage or keeping animals such as cattle.
An arena.
senses.example: Maple Leaf Gardens was a grand old barn.

senses.definition: A warm and cozy place, especially a bedroom; a roost.
A unit of surface area equal to 10 square meters.
To lay up in a barn.

core.definition: A large farm building used to store hay and grain or to shelter livestock.

pronunciation.tip: Keep it to one syllable with a clear r and the vowel of car. Do not add an extra vowel between the r and the n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and rural; it suggests farm life and a homey, practical feel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use barn for the large building on a farm, often red and wooden, and for horse shelters in some areas, though many people say stable for a building used only for horses. Phrases like barn dance and barn-raising, a community building event, are common in American culture. A city dweller might call a large storage building a barn, but the word usually means a farm building.

distinctions.note: A stable is usually for keeping horses, while a barn can hold hay, equipment and many kinds of animals.
A shed is smaller and usually for tools or storage; a barn is larger and often part of a working farm.

examples.everyday: We drove past the old red barn on the way to the lake.
examples.professional: The inspector said the barn needs a new roof before winter, so we should get a quote this week.
examples.analytical: In Luke 12:18 the rich man plans to pull down his barns and build larger ones, a picture of security based on storage.

nuance.analogy: A barn is the farm's storage closet, big enough to hold the whole season's harvest.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bern, from bere, barley, and ern, building, so originally a barley house.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel or lengthening the vowel, as in BAIRN or BAR-en.
Saying the barn when speaking about barns in general; use barns in the plural for a general idea.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the barn stands for stored wealth and self-reliance. Jesus tells the parable of the rich fool in Luke 12:16-21, who plans to tear down his barns and build bigger ones, and God calls him a fool that night. Matthew 6:26 notes that the birds neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, yet God feeds them, and Matthew 13:30 has the wheat gathered into the barn at harvest in the parable of the wheat and weeds.

barn.etymology: From Middle English *barn*, *bern*, *bærn*, from Old English *bearn*, *bern*, contracted forms of Old English *berern*, *bereærn* (“barn, granary”), compound of *bere* (“barley”) and *ærn*, *ræn* (“dwelling, barn”), from **raʀn*, from Proto-Germanic…

senses.definition: A basis or foundation.
senses.example: If culture is the bedrock of a society, then language is the cornerstone of culture.

senses.definition: The bones.
The solid rock found at some depth below the ground surface.
To establish on a solid foundation.

core.definition: The basic principles or foundation on which something is built; the solid base that everything else depends on.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BED, with a lighter secondary stress on rock. The vowel in 'rock' is the open 'ah' sound used by most Americans, so it rhymes with 'lock' and not with 'lark'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests stability, reliability, and strength, so it is a favorable word for beliefs, values, or finances.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bedrock often in politics, business, and everyday conversation to describe what something is really built on, such as 'bedrock values' or 'the bedrock of our economy'. In casual speech, it can also mean the lowest possible level, as in 'prices hit bedrock'. The literal geological meaning is less common in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Foundation is more general and can be literal or figurative, while bedrock stresses the most basic and solid layer that nothing lies beneath.
A cornerstone is one important part that a structure is built around, while bedrock describes the entire base that supports everything.
Basis is a neutral, slightly abstract word, while bedrock adds a vivid sense of solidity and strength.

examples.everyday: Honesty is bedrock for me, so I don't care how much money a friend offers if they lie to me.
examples.professional: Our reliability and uptime are the bedrock of this platform, so we should not sacrifice them for new features.
examples.analytical: For many early American republicans, the rule of law was the bedrock on which every other liberty depended.

nuance.analogy: Like the solid stone under a building that keeps the walls from sinking into the soil.
nuance.etymology: From bed in the sense of a layer, plus rock, meaning the solid layer of rock lying beneath soil.
common_mistakes: Using it only as a literal word for rock beneath the surface, when the figurative sense is more common.
Pronouncing the vowel in 'rock' with a long 'o' sound, as in 'rope'.
Confusing it with 'bottom', which lacks the sense of solid strength.

senses.definition: A section of a written work containing citations, not quotations, to all the books referred to in the work.
A list of books or documents relevant to a particular subject or author.
The study of the history of books in terms of their classification, printing and publication.

core.definition: A list of books, articles, and other sources cited in a work, or recommended for a particular subject or author.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AH, the second-to-last-but-one syllable, so the sound is 'bib-lee-AH-gruh-fee'. Americans use the 'ah' vowel of the cot-caught merger, and the -ra- is a quick 'ruh', not 'rah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scholarly. It signals careful research and sourcing.
nuance.usage_note: Students, researchers, and professionals use 'bibliography' in papers, theses, and reports, although in US academic writing the list is often called 'references' or 'works cited' depending on the style guide. Asking someone for 'a bibliography on the topic' is natural and polite, meaning a list of recommended readings. In everyday talk it may be shortened to 'reading list'.

distinctions.note: References usually lists only the sources you actually cited, often in APA style, while a bibliography can include sources you read but did not cite.
A reading list is a course or teacher's list of assigned or recommended texts, usually less formal than a bibliography.

examples.everyday: I asked the librarian for a bibliography on World War II, and she gave me a printed list of books.
examples.professional: Please add the full bibliography to the appendix before we send the report to legal.
examples.analytical: A good bibliography reveals a scholar's intellectual debts as clearly as the footnotes do.

nuance.analogy: Like a restaurant's ingredient list, it shows where the work came from.
nuance.etymology: From Greek biblion, 'book', plus -graphia, 'writing'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as 'BIB-lee-og-ruh-fee' instead of bib-lee-AH-gruh-fee.
Using 'bibliography' for a short list of two or three books, which is usually just 'references' or 'sources'.
Confusing the noun with the adjective 'bibliographic' in phrases like 'bibliography information'.

bibliography.etymology: From Ancient Greek *βιβλιογραφία* (“the act or habit of writing books”), from *βιβλιογράφος* (“a writer of books”), from *βιβλίον* (“small book”) + *γράφω* (“I write”).

senses.definition: Lacking piety or respect for the sacred; resembling blasphemy.
senses.example: His taking the name of God in vain was considered blasphemous.

core.definition: Showing great disrespect toward God or something considered sacred, or treating holy things with contempt.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the word has only three syllables, so the ending sounds like 'mus', not 'mous'. The ph is pronounced as an f.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. Calling something blasphemous is a serious moral accusation, though it is sometimes used loosely for anything outrageous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in religious discussions, sermons, and news about art, films, or speech that offends believers. In casual talk people sometimes use it loosely, as in 'That's blasphemous!' to mean outrageous, which can sound exaggerated. In religious settings it is a serious word, so avoid it when you only mean rude or offensive.

distinctions.note: Profane describes something irreverent or vulgar in general, while blasphemous specifically targets God or sacred things.
Sacrilegious refers to violating something sacred, especially a holy place or object, while blasphemous focuses on insulting God or holy things in words or attitude.

examples.everyday: Some people at church said the movie was blasphemous, but I thought it was just a dark comedy.
examples.professional: Our legal team reviewed the ad campaign to make sure no image could be seen as blasphemous to any faith group.
examples.analytical: Medieval critics treated certain doctrinal claims as blasphemous not because they insulted a person, but because they seemed to deny God's unique nature.

nuance.analogy: Like touching a sacred object without respect: the act itself crosses a line that many people believe should never be crossed.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin blasphemus, from Greek blasphemos 'speaking evil', from blasphemein.
common_mistakes: Saying 'blas-FEE-mous' with a long e; the stress is on the first syllable and the vowel is short.
Using 'blasphemous' loosely for anything rude; in English it has a strong religious meaning.
Adding an extra syllable, as in 'blas-fuh-muh-us'; say it in three syllables, BLAS-fuh-mus.

blasphemous.etymology: From Latin *blasphēmus* (“blaspheming”), from Ancient Greek *βλάσφημος* (“uttering ill-omened words”), equivalent to *blaspheme* + *ous*.

senses.definition: In blasphemous manner.

core.definition: In a way that shows contempt or disrespect toward God or something considered sacred.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllables reduce to a weak uh sound. Don't insert an extra vowel between the s and the f, and keep the final -ly as a light lee.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; it accuses someone of disrespect toward sacred things, so it is serious rather than casual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this adverb in everyday speech; it appears mostly in religious, literary or journalistic writing. In conversation people more often use the adjective blasphemous or the noun blasphemy, sometimes jokingly. Using it for mild exaggeration sounds odd and can seem like an overreaction.

distinctions.note: Profane language involves swearing or vulgarity; blasphemous speech specifically insults God or sacred things.
Sacrilege violates something sacred, often a place or object, while blasphemy is verbal or written contempt for the sacred.

examples.everyday: My uncle joked blasphemously about the church picnic, and my aunt just shook her head.
examples.professional: The reviewer described the novel's ending as written so blasphemously that readers flooded the publisher with angry emails.
examples.analytical: The author treats the crucifixion so blasphemously that the scene reads as satire of religious hypocrisy rather than an attack on faith.

nuance.analogy: Like spitting into the punch bowl at a wedding: the act is aimed straight at what everyone holds sacred.
nuance.etymology: From Greek blasphēmein, to speak evil of, from blasphēmos, speaking impiously.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for rudely or harshly in ordinary complaints; it refers specifically to disrespect toward the sacred.
Stressing the second syllable instead of BLAS at the start of the word.

senses.definition: A mixture of two or more things.
senses.example: Their music has been described as a blend of jazz and heavy metal.

senses.definition: A word formed by combining two other words; a portmanteau word.
To mingle; to mix; to unite intimately; to pass or shade insensibly into each other.
senses.example: To make hummus you need to blend chickpeas, olive oil, lemon juice and garlic.

senses.definition: To be mingled or mixed.
