core.definition: Noun: a mixture of two or more different things combined into one. Verb: to mix two or more things so they become one whole.

pronunciation.tip: This is a one-syllable word with a short e as in 'bed'. Pronounce the final d clearly and do not add an extra vowel before it, as in 'blen-duh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. A blend is usually seen as a good combination, as in coffee, tea, fabric, or a team that works well together.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'blend' often in everyday contexts, especially about food and drinks: a fruit smoothie is often called a blend, and a 'blended coffee' is a drink mixed with ice. In professional speech, 'blend' can mean combining methods or approaches, as in 'a blended learning program'. You can also say 'blend in' to mean fitting in with a group.

distinctions.note: 'Mix' is the general word for putting things together. 'Blend' suggests the parts become more uniform and hard to separate.
'Combination' is more formal and abstract and can refer to a set of things, while 'blend' describes a more physical or intimate mixture.

collocations: a blend of old and new

examples.everyday: Can you blend the strawberries and bananas for the smoothie?
examples.professional: Our team uses a blend of agile and waterfall methods, depending on the project.
examples.analytical: Her theory is a blend of Aristotelian ethics and modern utilitarian reasoning, which makes it difficult to classify neatly.

nuance.analogy: Like paint colors stirred together until you cannot see the original shades, a blend merges separate things into one.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English blenden, from Old English blandan, meaning to mix.
common_mistakes: Using 'blend' for a simple mixing of two separate parts that stay visible; 'mix' is more natural there.
Saying 'blend with' when the phrasal verb is 'blend in with' or 'blend into' to mean fitting in.

blend.etymology: From Middle English *blenden*, either from Old English *blandan*, *blondan*, *ġeblandan*, *ġeblendan* or from Old Norse *blanda* (“to blend, mix”) (which was originally a strong verb with the present-tense stem *blend*; compare *blendingr* (“a blending, a…

conversation.text: Blend the fruit and yogurt to make a smoothie.
Blend the soup until it's smooth.
I blended some spinach into the smoothie.

senses.definition: A search algorithm that begins at the root node and explores all the neighboring nodes.

core.definition: A graph or tree search algorithm that explores all nodes at one level before moving to nodes at the next level.

pronunciation.tip: The compound is usually stressed on breadth and search, with first often lighter in speech. Do not pronounce the r in first as a separate syllable, and make the vowel in search an r-colored sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used in computer science and AI.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use breadth-first search in computer science courses, technical interviews and code reviews, usually with the abbreviation BFS. In casual speech people rarely say the full phrase. It contrasts with depth-first search, which goes deep down one path before backtracking.

distinctions.note: Depth-first search explores one branch as far as possible before backtracking, while breadth-first search explores level by level.
Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths in weighted graphs, while breadth-first search finds shortest paths only when all edges have equal cost.

collocations: use a queue for breadth-first search

examples.everyday: My friend is studying for interviews and keeps explaining breadth-first search to me over dinner.
examples.professional: In the code review, I suggested switching to breadth-first search because it guarantees the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
examples.analytical: Breadth-first search is optimal for unweighted graphs, since it reaches every node at distance k before any node at distance k plus one.

nuance.analogy: Breadth-first search is like ripples spreading from a stone in a pond, reaching every point at one distance before moving outward.
nuance.etymology: Breadth comes from Old English brād, broad; first from Old English fyrst; search from Old French cerchier.
common_mistakes: Confusing breadth-first search with depth-first search and using the wrong one for shortest path problems.
Saying the phrase as three separate stressed words without the hyphen in writing.

conversation.text: Breadth-first search explores all nodes at one depth before moving to the next level.
On an unweighted graph, breadth-first search finds a shortest path, but it can use a lot of memory.
Use breadth-first search here so we find the closest related account first.

senses.definition: To begin suddenly; to emerge in a certain condition.
senses.example: He broke out in sweat.

senses.definition: To suddenly get pimples or a rash, especially on one's face.
senses.example: break out in hives

senses.definition: To escape, especially forcefully or defiantly.
senses.example: They broke out of prison in the middle of the night.

senses.definition: To rescue someone or aid their escape as in sense 1.
senses.example: After Big Tony was sent to prison, his friends got together to break him out.

senses.definition: To bring out from storage, use, or present.
senses.example: Break out the bubbly and celebrate.

senses.definition: To separate (something) from a bundle.
senses.example: Break out the cables from the harness once they are inside the frame.

senses.definition: To take or force out by breaking.
senses.example: to break out a pane of glass

senses.definition: (Of a record, film, product, or company): to achieve widespread success.
senses.example: It wasn't until later that her album broke out and she hit the big time.

core.definition: To start suddenly, such as a fire, war or argument, or to escape from a place by force.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on out, which carries the main meaning. The ou is a diphthong, so say 'owt' with a clear 'ow' sound, not 'oot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It usually describes sudden trouble or unwanted events, though it can also describe a sudden success or breakthrough.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say a fight broke out at the bar, or a fire broke out in the kitchen, in everyday talk. For skin, people say I broke out in a rash or my son broke out in pimples. In news writing, break out of prison describes an escape. Breaking out in a sweat is also common informal speech.

distinctions.note: Start is neutral and general, while break out emphasizes something sudden, often unexpected or unwanted.
Erupt is more dramatic and emotional, while break out is common in everyday speech for trouble, illness or events.

examples.everyday: A fight broke out at the game last night, so the security guards had to step in.
examples.professional: A bug broke out in production this morning, and the on-call team is working on a fix now.
examples.analytical: Historians debate why the war broke out, since the conditions for conflict were present for many years before the first shots.

nuance.analogy: When a fire breaks out, it is like a dam giving way: the pressure builds quietly and then bursts into the open all at once.
nuance.etymology: From Old English brecan, to break, plus out, meaning to come forth or emerge.
common_mistakes: Using break out for slow changes; it describes a sudden start.
Mixing up break out of with break into; break out means to escape from, while break into means to enter forcibly.

conversation.text: A fight broke out in the parking lot after the game.
Two prisoners broke out of the county jail last night.
I always break out when I eat too much chocolate.
Let's break out the good wine, it's a special night.

core.definition: In the New Testament, the early Christian practice of sharing meals together, closely linked to the Lord's Supper.

pronunciation.tip: Both bread and breaking are stressed, with bread getting the main stress. Of reduces to uv or a quick schwa, and bread rhymes with said.

nuance.connotation: Warm and reverent, suggesting fellowship and holy simplicity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this mostly in church, Bible study and writing about early Christianity. It echoes Acts 2:42. Outside religion, people say break bread together to mean share a meal in friendship, which is a common idiom.

distinctions.note: The Lord's Supper is the specific rite; the breaking of bread can mean ordinary meals as well as the rite.
Eucharist is the later liturgical term; breaking of bread is the New Testament phrase.
The idiom means simply to eat together, often to make peace or build friendship.

collocations: fellowship and the breaking of bread
devoted to the breaking of bread

examples.everyday: It would be great to sit down and break bread with you and your family sometime.
examples.professional: Tonight's lesson looks at why the first believers made the breaking of bread central to their life.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the breaking of bread in Acts refers to ordinary meals, the Eucharist, or both.

nuance.analogy: Like a shared family table, where eating together binds people.
nuance.etymology: Old English brecan and brēad; the phrase translates Greek klasis tou artou.
common_mistakes: Saying breaking bread without of when the noun phrase is needed.
Taking the idiom literally as breaking a loaf only.
Pronouncing bread like breed.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek phrase is klasis tou artou, the breaking of bread. Acts 2:42 says the believers devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayers. Acts 2:46 says they broke bread in their homes. In Luke 24:30-35 the disciples recognize the risen Jesus when he breaks the bread, and Acts 20:7 records believers gathering on the first day of the week to break bread.

senses.definition: An ongoing problem; a recurring obstacle or adversity.
A source of dread; resentment; or irritation.
A generic creature, often described as a large goblin, meant to inspire fear in children.
To alarm with idle phantoms. (clarification of this definition is needed)

core.definition: A persistent problem or worry that keeps causing irritation or difficulty over a long period.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: BUG-bair. The final syllable sounds like 'bare' with an American r, not 'bee-ar,' and the word is one word.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something annoying that keeps coming back.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bugbear more in writing or formal talk than in casual speech, so it sounds slightly dressed up. You might say 'The biggest bugbear for our team is the old database.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, that's a bugbear for us too.' Use it to name a recurring frustration without sounding overly angry.

distinctions.note: A pet peeve is a small personal annoyance, while a bugbear can be a larger recurring problem that affects a group.
A headache is an informal word for any trouble, while bugbear suggests a long-running issue you keep meeting.
A bottleneck is a point that slows a process, while a bugbear is any recurring problem, not necessarily one in a flow.

examples.everyday: Slow Wi-Fi is my biggest bugbear, especially when I'm working from home.
examples.professional: Flaky test data remains the team's bugbear, and it keeps delaying our model retraining.
examples.analytical: For many theologians, the problem of evil remains a bugbear that resists neat resolution within any single doctrine.

nuance.analogy: A bugbear is like a loose floorboard: you step over it every day, and it still catches your foot now and then.
nuance.etymology: From bug, a goblin or bogey, plus bear; the goblin sense is older than the modern meaning of a recurring problem.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, bug bear; it is one word.
Thinking it refers to an animal; it means a recurring source of annoyance.

senses.definition: The duty of a party in a legal proceeding to prove an assertion of fact; it includes both the burden of production and the burden of persuasion; the onus probandi.
The obligation of the person making a claim in a dispute to provide sufficient evidence for their position.

core.definition: The obligation of a person making a claim to provide enough evidence to support it, or the legal duty to prove a fact in court.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BUR in 'burden' and on PROOF. The word 'of' is reduced to a weak 'uhv', and the vowel in 'proof' is the 'oo' of 'roof', not 'puh-ruff'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a neutral term for who must provide evidence, and it can sound pointed when used in an argument.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the burden of proof is on you' in arguments, debates, and meetings to push someone to back up a claim. It is firm but not rude when used in a discussion about evidence. In casual talk, people often say 'you're the one making the claim' instead.

distinctions.note: Burden of proof is who must prove something. Standard of proof is how much evidence is required, such as 'beyond a reasonable doubt'.
Onus is a formal synonym meaning responsibility or duty, often used in the phrase 'the onus is on'. Burden of proof is more specific to evidence.
Presumption is an assumption that something is true until shown otherwise. Burden of proof is the duty to show that it is or is not true.

collocations: the burden of proof lies with

examples.everyday: You said the coffee shop has the best bagels, but the burden of proof is on you to back that up.
examples.professional: In the model review, the burden of proof is on whoever claims the new version beats the baseline, so bring the test results.
examples.analytical: The burden of proof rests with those who assert a positive existence claim rather than with those who withhold belief.

nuance.analogy: Like a plaintiff in a courtroom who must bring the evidence to the jury, rather than the defendant who must disprove it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English byrthen (burden) and Old French prueve (proof), combined in legal English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'proof burden' or 'burden of prove' instead of 'burden of proof'
Confusing it with standard of proof, which is about how much evidence is enough

senses.definition: An audible signal to the calling party that indicates failure to complete the requested connection; an engaged tone.

core.definition: A repeating tone you hear on a phone when the number you called is already in use.

pronunciation.tip: Busy is pronounced BIZ-ee, not BOO-zee, with a short i as in 'is'. The stress is on the first word, and the second word is weaker.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical-sounding everyday term that means the line is in use.
nuance.usage_note: Older Americans still use busy signal, and people sometimes say 'I got a busy signal' or 'the line was busy'. Today most people just say the line was busy or that the call went to voicemail. It is not rude to report one.

distinctions.note: Ringing means the phone is calling the other person. A busy signal means the line is already in use and the call cannot connect.
Voicemail means the call connected and went to a recorded message. A busy signal means the call did not connect at all.

collocations: the line gave a busy signal

examples.everyday: I kept calling the doctor's office, but I only got a busy signal all morning.
examples.professional: When the vendor line gives a busy signal, please leave a message on the shared support queue.
examples.analytical: A busy signal reveals the limits of an older network, since it indicates capacity rather than failure to reach the person.

nuance.analogy: A busy signal is like a closed door that tells you someone is already inside, so you have to try again later.
nuance.etymology: Busy comes from Old English bisig. Signal comes from Old French signal, from Latin signum, a sign.
common_mistakes: Saying 'busy tone' or 'busy phone', which are not standard terms for this sound.
Pronouncing busy as BOO-zee, which is a common mistake for learners.

conversation.text: I keep getting a busy signal; she must be on the phone.
Back in the day, a busy signal meant you had to try later.
The office line gave me a busy signal all morning.

senses.definition: Peaceful, quiet, especially free from anger and anxiety.
Free of noise and disturbance.
With few or no waves on the surface; not rippled.
Without wind or storm.
Good; alright; cool; OK.
The state of being calm; peacefulness; absence of worry, anger, fear or other strong negative emotion.
The state of being calm; absence of noise and disturbance.
The absence of wind; a period of time without wind.
To make calm.
senses.example: to calm a crying baby

senses.definition: To become calm.

core.definition: Relaxed and quiet, not upset, angry, worried, or anxious, even in a difficult situation.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable with an open 'ah' vowel. The l is silent in General American, so say 'kahm,' not 'kahlm.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. Being calm is usually admired, especially in emergencies or stressful moments.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use calm constantly in everyday speech, such as 'Stay calm' or 'Just stay calm, it's fine.' It can also describe water, weather, or a quiet place. A natural reply to someone who says 'Calm down' is 'I am calm!' or 'Okay, sorry.' Be careful, because telling someone to calm down can sound condescending when they are upset.

distinctions.note: Quiet refers to low sound, while calm describes a peaceful emotional state or a still environment.
Relaxed suggests comfortable ease, while calm emphasizes the absence of agitation, especially in a tense situation.

examples.everyday: Stay calm, the dog won't bite if you don't move too fast.
examples.professional: Even when the production server went down, she stayed calm and walked the team through the rollback.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that a calm mind is not the absence of passion but the mastery of it.

nuance.analogy: Calm is like a lake on a windless morning, where the surface is smooth and nothing is disturbed.
nuance.etymology: From Old French calme, from Medieval Latin cauma, from Greek kauma, 'great heat.' The meaning shifted from heat to a period of stillness.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the l, as in 'kahlm.'
Saying 'I am calm' to mean 'I am calm down,' when calm down is a phrasal verb needing its particle.

calm.etymology: From Middle English *calm*, *calme*, from Middle French *calme*, probably from *calma*, of origin.

conversation.text: Try to stay calm. We'll figure it out.
She was surprisingly calm after the accident.
The ocean was really calm this morning, perfect for swimming.

senses.definition: An area where tents are pitched.
An area where a camp meeting (a retreat) is held.

core.definition: An outdoor area with sites where people can pitch tents, park RVs, and stay overnight, often with shared facilities.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAMP. The second syllable has the 'ow' sound of 'ground', not 'grand' or 'grownd'. Keep the p clear before the g.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests outdoor recreation and affordable overnight stays.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use campground for public and private camping areas, including state and national parks and RV parks. It is a common word on signs, maps, and reservation websites. You might say 'Let's find a campground near the lake.' A natural reply is 'Great, do they take reservations?'

distinctions.note: A campsite is one specific spot within a campground, while a campground is the whole area with many sites.
An RV park is mainly for recreational vehicles with hookups, while a campground usually serves tents and other camping setups too.
Camp can mean a summer program for kids or a temporary outdoor shelter, while campground specifically means a place to camp.

examples.everyday: We drove four hours to a campground by the lake, but the site was already full, so we ended up driving another hour.
examples.professional: The offsite team booked a campground near the conference venue, which made the trip cheaper for everyone.
examples.analytical: Campgrounds reflect a historical shift in American leisure, as public lands became shared spaces for families and recreation.

nuance.analogy: A campground is like a neighborhood for tents and RVs: many temporary homes share the same space for a night or a week.
nuance.etymology: Camp from Latin campus, 'field'; ground from Old English grund, 'bottom or surface of the earth'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'camping ground' as the only option; both are used, but campground is more common in American English.
Misplacing the stress on the second syllable, as in 'camp-GROUND'.
Confusing campground with campsite; one campground contains many campsites.

conversation.text: The campground has showers and clean restrooms.
Is the campground full, or can we just show up?
We stayed at a campground right next to the lake.

senses.definition: A polite way to ask to interrupt with a comment.

core.definition: A polite way to ask to interrupt a conversation or meeting in order to add a comment or idea.

pronunciation.tip: The words blend together so 'can I' sounds like 'kan-eye' and 'jump in' sounds like 'JUMP-in'. The main stress is on JUMP, and 'in' is light, so do not say a strong 'IN'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and collaborative when you wait for a pause; it can sound pushy if you interrupt mid-sentence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in team meetings, video calls, and friendly discussions to join a conversation that is moving quickly. Say it when someone pauses or just before you speak, and it is usually welcomed. Pair it with a short reason, such as 'Can I jump in with a quick point on the data?' Saying 'Sorry to interrupt' first is also common and polite.

distinctions.note: 'Jump in' sounds more energetic and collaborative, while 'add something' is more neutral and formal.
'Sorry to interrupt' apologizes for breaking the flow; 'can I jump in' asks for a turn more directly.

examples.everyday: We were talking about weekend plans, and I said, can I jump in? I'd love to come along.
examples.professional: During the sprint review, I said, can I jump in? The model's accuracy dropped after the last deployment.
examples.analytical: Asking to 'jump in' acknowledges the group's turn-taking norms and requests entry into the conversation without overriding it.

nuance.analogy: Like waiting for a gap in traffic before merging onto the highway.
nuance.etymology: 'Jump' comes from Middle English jumpen, of uncertain origin; 'in' is an adverb meaning into a space or activity.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Can I jump to you' or 'Can I jump on it', which mean different things.
Stressing 'in' too strongly, which sounds unnatural.

conversation.text: Can I jump in for a second? I have an update on that.
Sorry, can I jump in? That's not quite what happened.
"Can I jump in here?" "Sure, go ahead."

senses.definition: A waterfall or series of small waterfalls.
A stream or sequence of a thing or things occurring as if falling like a cascade.
senses.example: The bride carried a cascade of roses and baby's breath.

senses.definition: A series of electrical (or other types of) components, the output of any one being connected to the input of the next.
A pattern typically performed with an odd number of props, where each prop is caught by the opposite hand.

A sequence of absurd short messages posted to a newsgroup by different authors, each one responding to the most recent message and quoting the entire sequence to that point (with ever-increasing indentation).
A hairpiece for women consisting of curled locks or a bun attached to a firm base, used to create the illusion of fuller hair.
(chemistry) A series of reactions in which the product of one becomes a reactant in the next.
To fall as a waterfall or series of small waterfalls.
To arrange in a stepped series like a waterfall.
To occur as a causal sequence.
To pass (something) down through a chain or system in a flow or series of movements.

core.definition: A waterfall or series of small waterfalls, or anything that pours or tumbles downward in a similar way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, on the 'kayd' sound. The first vowel is short, as in 'cat', not a long 'kay' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing beauty, as in a cascade of light. It can be negative in technical or crisis contexts, such as a cascade failure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cascade for water, but also for things that arrive or fall in large amounts, such as emails, hair, or notifications. It sounds slightly polished in speech, so a casual speaker might say 'a bunch of' instead. In tech news, 'cascade failure' is a common phrase.

distinctions.note: A waterfall is usually one big drop, while a cascade is a series of smaller falls or a flow that tumbles in steps.
A torrent is a violent, fast rush of water, while cascade emphasizes falling in tiers.
Flood suggests overflowing and overwhelming, while cascade describes a more orderly, tiered flow.

examples.everyday: Wow, look at that cascade of water coming over the rocks at the park.
examples.professional: Our monitoring dashboard showed a cascade of alerts right after the database went down.
examples.analytical: Each premise in his argument rests on the one before it, so a single flaw sets off a cascade of collapse.

nuance.analogy: Like a staircase made of water, with each pool spilling into the next one below.
nuance.etymology: From French cascade, from Italian cascata, from cascare 'to fall', from Vulgar Latin *cadicare.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (KAS-cayd); the stress belongs on the second syllable.
Using cascade for a single large waterfall; Americans usually say waterfall for that.

cascade.etymology: From French *cascade*, from Italian *cascata*, from *cascare* (“to fall”), from Vulgar Latin **cāsicāre*, derived from Latin *cadō*, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **ḱh₂d-*.

senses.definition: An inversion of the relationship between the elements of phrases.

core.definition: A figure of speech in which the second half of a phrase reverses the order of words or ideas in the first half.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the middle syllable, AZ, with a short a as in cat. The final -mus sounds like the word muss, and the ending is unstressed and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds polished and rhetorical, so it can seem showy if used in casual conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chiasmus mainly in English class, literary analysis, speechwriting, and biblical scholarship. Speakers rarely say it in everyday conversation, but they may point out a memorable line like Kennedy's Ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country. Use it when you want to name the technique, not as a general word for repetition.

distinctions.note: Antithesis sets two opposing ideas side by side, while chiasmus specifically reverses the grammatical or verbal order of the repeated elements.
Parallelism repeats the same structure in the same order, while chiasmus repeats it in reverse order, creating an ABBA pattern.

examples.everyday: Work to live, don't live to work. That's a chiasmus, and it's why people remember the slogan.
examples.professional: Clean data makes good models, and good models need clean data, so the slide's chiasmus makes our priority easy to remember.
examples.analytical: Kennedy's inaugural line uses chiasmus to turn a civic demand into a reversed, memorable obligation of citizenship.

nuance.analogy: Like a mirror image: the second half reflects the first half in reverse order.
nuance.etymology: From Greek khiasmos ('crossing'), from khiazein, 'to mark with the letter chi (X)'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a ch sound as in chair; the first sound is k.
Using chiasmus to mean any repeated phrase; the structure must reverse the order.
Confusing it with chiasm, the anatomical term for a crossing, such as the optic chiasm, which is a different sense.

senses.definition: In a clamorous manner.

core.definition: In a very loud, insistent way, with a lot of noise or demanding attention.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the middle syllables weak. Pronounce the final 'ly' as 'lee', and do not add an extra syllable between 'us' and 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes loud, insistent behavior, often with an impression of disorder or pressure.
nuance.usage_note: 'Clamorously' is rare in spoken American English and appears mostly in literary writing or formal descriptions. In conversation, Americans would say 'loudly' or 'noisily'. Use it sparingly, because it sounds dramatic.

distinctions.note: 'Loudly' is everyday and neutral about volume, while 'clamorously' suggests insistence or demands.
'Noisily' describes making noise in general, while 'clamorously' implies a crowd or demand that is pressing for attention.

examples.everyday: The phone kept ringing clamorously until someone finally picked it up.
examples.professional: The stakeholders clamorously demanded a revised timeline, so we had to rebuild the schedule.
examples.analytical: The reformers clamorously insisted on immediate change, though the historical record suggests slower processes.

nuance.analogy: Acting clamorously is like a fire alarm that refuses to stop until someone responds.
nuance.etymology: From clamorous, from clamor, from Latin clamor 'outcry', with the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'clamorously' in everyday speech where 'loudly' is more natural.
Confusing 'clamorously' with 'clamorously' as a noun-like phrase; it modifies verbs or adjectives only.

senses.definition: Synonym of nickname, any epithet used similar to the Roman cognomina.
Synonym of surname, a family name.
A personal epithet or clan name added to the given name and family name of Ancient Romans.
senses.example: Julius Caesar's actual name was Gaius Iulius Caesar. Gaius was his praenomen or forename, Iulius his nomen or surname, and Caesar his cognomen, denoting which part of the Iulius family he belonged to.

core.definition: A nickname or family name; in ancient Rome, the third name that identified a particular family branch, such as the 'Cicero' in Marcus Tullius Cicero.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, kahg-NOH-mun. The final syllable is weak, so say 'mun', not 'men'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds scholarly, and using it in ordinary talk can sound showy or humorous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in daily life. You will see it in history, classics, and literature, or when someone wants to sound witty about a nickname. In everyday talk, say 'nickname' or 'last name'. Calling a surname a 'cognomen' sounds pretentious unless the context is historical or playful.

distinctions.note: A nickname is informal and personal; a cognomen is formal and, in the Roman sense, a hereditary family or branch name.
A surname is the ordinary term for a family name in modern English; 'cognomen' is a rare, literary or historical synonym.

collocations: a cognomen inscribed on the monument

examples.everyday: Everyone at the office calls him Sarge, so I guess that's his cognomen now.
examples.professional: In the historical section of the report, we should cite the cognomen as it appears in the original Latin inscription.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the cognomen signaled a hereditary family branch or an individual achievement.

nuance.analogy: A cognomen is like a family nickname that gets written into the official record and passed down.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cognomen, from co- 'with' plus (g)nomen 'name'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'COG-no-men'.
Using it as a casual synonym for 'nickname' in modern conversation.
Pronouncing the last syllable as 'men' instead of 'mun'.

senses.definition: A one-piece form of underwear, being a combination of a vest or chemise and underpants.

core.definition: Possible groups or selections formed by choosing items from a larger set, where the order does not matter.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -NAY-, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, so say 'buh', not 'bih'. The 'sh' sound is a single sound, and the word ends with a z sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is value-free, though in statistics it has a precise meaning.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, combinations usually means ways things are put together, like a combination of flavors or the codes for a lock. In statistics it counts selections where order does not matter, so the phrase 'the number of combinations' is common. The old sense of one-piece underwear (a combination or combo) is dated and rarely used today.

distinctions.note: Permutations count arrangements where order matters; combinations count selections where order does not.
A set is a collection of items; combinations are the smaller groups you can form by choosing from that set.

examples.everyday: There are a lot of possible combinations for that lock, so I can't just guess the code.
examples.professional: We need to test all combinations of browser and operating system before the release.
examples.analytical: The number of combinations grows so quickly with the size of the set that brute force soon becomes impractical.

nuance.analogy: Like choosing two toppings for a pizza: the order you name them doesn't change the pizza.
nuance.etymology: From Latin combinatio, from combinare 'to join together'.
common_mistakes: Confusing combinations with permutations; in combinations order does not matter, but in permutations it does.
Using combinations for a single mixture; say 'a combination of' for one mixed thing, and 'combinations' for the set of possibilities.

senses.definition: A process whereby two chemicals are combined to produce heat.
A process wherein a fuel is combined with oxygen, usually at high temperature, releasing heat.
(chemistry) The act or process of burning.
Violent agitation, tumult.

core.definition: The process of burning, in which a fuel combines rapidly with oxygen and releases heat and light.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BUS. In American English the '-tion' ending is pronounced 'chun', not 'shun', because the t blends into the ch sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a scientific term with no emotional charge. People sometimes use it loosely in phrases like spontaneous combustion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use combustion mainly in science, engineering and automotive contexts, as in 'internal combustion engine.' In everyday conversation they say burning or fire. Spontaneous combustion is a popular phrase for something catching fire without an outside flame, and people often use it loosely. Use combustion in writing and presentations; say burning in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Burning is the everyday word for something on fire; combustion names the chemical process that produces heat and light.
Oxidation is a broader category of reactions; combustion is rapid oxidation that releases heat and light.

examples.everyday: The fire pit is smoky because it needs more air for good combustion.
examples.professional: The engineering team wants to cut emissions by improving combustion efficiency in the turbine.
examples.analytical: Lavoisier's account of combustion as oxygen combining with a substance overturned the older phlogiston theory.

nuance.analogy: Combustion is like a chain of falling dominoes: each reaction sets off the next and releases energy.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin combustio, from Latin comburere 'to burn up', from com- 'together' and urere 'to burn'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as in KOM-bus-tion instead of kuhm-BUS-chun.
Using combustion to mean a flammable material; combustion is the process, and combustible is the material.

combustion.etymology: From Old French *combustion*, from Latin *combustio*, from *comburere* (“to burn”), itself from the intensifying prefix com- + the root burere; equivalent to *combust* + *ion*.

senses.definition: The property of a logical theory that whenever a wff is valid then it must also be a theorem. Symbolically, letting T represent a theory within logic L, this can be represented as the property that whenever T⊨ϕ is true, then T⊢ϕ must also be true, for any wff φ of logic L.
The state or condition of being complete.

core.definition: The condition of having all the necessary parts or information, with nothing missing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on PLEET. The -ness ending is weak, so say 'nus' with a reduced vowel, and keep the t in 'complete' from being fully released before the n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a quality of thoroughness, though in logic it has a precise technical meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use completeness in everyday talk about records and work, such as 'the completeness of the report.' In logic and mathematics, it is a technical term about whether a system can prove all true statements. Use the general sense in ordinary conversation and the logic sense only in specialized discussion.

distinctions.note: Completion is the act or moment of finishing. Completeness is the quality of having everything in place.
Thoroughness is careful, detailed work. Completeness is whether something has all its parts, even if the work was not very careful.

examples.everyday: I'm not sure about the completeness of the order, so can you double-check that everything arrived?
examples.professional: Before we publish, we need to verify the completeness of the dataset, especially the missing values in the last quarter.
examples.analytical: Gödel showed that no consistent formal system of arithmetic can prove its own completeness, which limits what mathematics can establish.

nuance.analogy: Like a jigsaw puzzle, which has completeness only when every piece is on the table.
nuance.etymology: From complete plus -ness, from Latin completus, filled up, finished.
common_mistakes: Confusing completeness with completion, which is the act of finishing.
Using it in the logic sense in everyday talk, where it sounds overly technical.

senses.definition: Hidden.
Of a meld; completed without calling another player's discarded tile unless that call would complete the hand.
Of a hand; completed with all concealed melds.

core.definition: Hidden or kept out of sight, so that it is not easily seen or noticed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SEELD, with a long ee vowel. Don't stress the first syllable or pronounce it with a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It becomes negative when it describes something deliberately hidden to deceive, such as a concealed fee or a concealed truth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use concealed for physical objects and information, as in 'a concealed weapon' or 'concealed under a jacket.' In everyday talk, 'hidden' is more common and casual. The phrase 'concealed carry' is a legal term in the US for carrying a hidden handgun with a permit.

distinctions.note: Hidden is the everyday word. Concealed suggests someone deliberately covered something up.
Secret describes information kept from others. Concealed describes a physical object or fact kept out of view.

examples.everyday: The kids hid the cookies, but the dog found them, so the concealed treats didn't last long.
examples.professional: The vendor's contract concealed a setup fee that only appeared on the first invoice.
examples.analytical: Many arguments about free will rest on causes concealed from introspection, so we infer them rather than observe them directly.

nuance.analogy: Like a key under a doormat: it is really there, just out of sight.
nuance.etymology: From Latin concelare, to hide completely, from com- (thoroughly) and celare (to hide).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (KON-seeld) instead of kun-SEELD
Using concealed as a noun for a hiding place; the noun is concealment

senses.definition: Stating that one sentence is true if another is true.
senses.example: "A implies B" is a conditional statement.

senses.definition: Limited by a condition.
senses.example: I made my son a conditional promise: I would buy him a bike if he kept his room tidy.

senses.definition: Expressing a condition or supposition.
senses.example: a conditional word, mode, or tense

senses.definition: A statement that one sentence is true if another is.
senses.example: "A implies B" is a conditional.

senses.definition: A conditional sentence; a statement that depends on a condition being true or false.
The conditional mood.
An instruction that branches depending on the truth of a condition at that point.
senses.example: if and while are conditionals in some programming languages.

senses.definition: A condition (a limitation or restriction).

core.definition: Depending on a condition: true or happening only if something else is true or happens, as in 'if this, then that'.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DISH, and the -tion is pronounced shun. Many learners pronounce the last syllable as al, but in fast American speech it sounds like nuhl.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in logic and statistics and a common everyday adjective meaning 'depending on.'
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, conditional usually means that something depends on a condition, as in 'My approval is conditional.' In math, logic, and statistics it describes statements of the form if P then Q, or probabilities that depend on another event. In grammar classes, conditional refers to sentences with if clauses.

distinctions.note: Contingent is close in meaning, but it is more formal and often means dependent on uncertain events, while conditional is more common in everyday and technical use.
Unconditional means without any requirement or limits, the direct opposite of conditional.

examples.everyday: My landlord gave us a conditional yes, as long as we pay the deposit by Friday.
examples.professional: The hiring offer is conditional on passing the background check and the security review.
examples.analytical: A conditional statement of the form if P then Q is false only when P is true and Q is false, which is why logicians treat it as material implication.

nuance.analogy: A conditional statement is like a vending machine: you get the snack only if you put in the right coins.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin conditionalis, from condicio, condition.
common_mistakes: Using conditional as a noun in everyday talk; the noun is more often a conditional sentence or conditional mood.
Confusing conditional with condition, the noun form that means a state or requirement.
Pronouncing the middle syllable too strongly as kun-DIH-shun-al; keep the -ion ending weak.

conditional.etymology: From French *conditionnel*, from Old French *condicionel*, equivalent to *condition* + *-al*.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of conference.

core.definition: A short, informal word for a conference, especially a large meeting or event.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable with a short, open o, like 'cot,' followed by a clear f. Do not add a vowel after the f.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a casual, shortened form used among colleagues or friends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conf mainly in casual speech and informal writing, such as in calendar entries or chat messages: 'Are you going to the conf next week?' In formal writing, use conference. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I'm registered.'

distinctions.note: Conference is the full, formal word for a meeting or event; conf is a casual abbreviation used mainly in speech and informal writing.
A meeting is usually a smaller gathering within an organization, while a conf is a larger event, often with multiple sessions.

examples.everyday: Are you going to the conf in Denver next month, or are you staying home?
examples.professional: I submitted a talk proposal for the data science conf, so let me know if you want to co-present.
examples.analytical: Academic conference culture increasingly depends on informal shorthand, though formal papers still use the full word.

nuance.analogy: A conf is like the nickname of a big event: everyone knows what it means, but the formal name appears on the badge.
nuance.etymology: Shortened from conference, from Latin conferre, to bring together.
common_mistakes: Using conf in formal writing or academic papers.
Pronouncing it with a long vowel like 'cone'.

senses.definition: A person who confounds.
A factor, in data analysis, that causes the effects of two distinct processes to be indistinguishable; a confounding variable.

core.definition: In statistics, a third variable linked to both the exposure and the outcome that distorts or hides the true relationship between them.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, FOWN, and the final -er is a reduced, rhotic sound, not a full 'ah'. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce the final vowel as a clear 'oo'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in statistics. In everyday speech, a 'confounder' is rare and can mean something that confuses or baffles a situation, which is a mild, slightly negative sense.
nuance.usage_note: In data science and epidemiology, Americans say confounder or confounding variable for a factor that must be controlled for. Outside technical work, you will rarely hear it, and 'confounding factor' or 'complication' is more natural. Use it precisely in research settings and avoid it in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Nearly identical in meaning. 'Confounder' is shorter and common in papers, while 'confounding variable' is more explicit for students and reports.
A mediator explains how an effect happens by sitting on the causal path, whereas a confounder sits outside that path and creates a spurious association.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the rain was the big confounder for our hiking plans, since it messed up everything we'd set up.
examples.professional: Before we trust the A/B test, we need to check whether user location is a confounder for both the feature rollout and the conversion rate.
examples.analytical: A confounder is a variable that is associated with both the exposure and the outcome without lying on the causal pathway between them, which is why stratification is needed.

nuance.analogy: A confounder is like a loud fan in a room where you are trying to hear a whisper: the noise makes it impossible to tell which sound really came from the speaker.
nuance.etymology: From confound, from Old French confondre, from Latin confundere, 'to pour together, mix up'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -er as a full 'ah' sound instead of a reduced American r-colored vowel.
Using 'confounder' to mean a person who confuses others in everyday speech, where it sounds unnatural.
Confusing a confounder with a mediator or a collider in causal reasoning.

senses.definition: A lineup or sequence of railroad carriages or cars, with or without a locomotive, that form a unit.
senses.example: The train's consist included a baggage car, four passenger cars, and a diner.

core.definition: To be made up of certain parts or elements; to be composed of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the second and only stressed syllable, SIST, which rhymes with 'list'. Do not add a vowel between s and t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is precise and works in all contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'consist of' in writing and formal speech to describe what something is made of, as in 'The team consists of five people.' In casual speech they often say 'is made up of' or 'includes' instead. It is never followed directly by a noun without 'of', except in the sense 'consist in' (to lie in).

distinctions.note: Consist of lists the complete makeup of something; include suggests the items are only part of a larger whole.
Comprise means to contain or be made of; in careful American writing, prefer 'comprises' for the whole and avoid 'is comprised of'.

examples.everyday: My lunch usually consists of a sandwich and an apple.
examples.professional: The dataset consists of roughly two million records, split into training and test sets.
examples.analytical: Aristotle held that a good life consists in the activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.

nuance.analogy: Like a sandwich, which is nothing more than its bread, filling, and sauce put together.
nuance.etymology: From Latin consistere, 'to stand together', from com- 'together' and sistere 'to stand'.
common_mistakes: Using 'consist' without 'of' in the sense of being made up of, as in 'The team consists five people'.
Using the continuous form, as in 'is consisting of'; it is a stative verb and is not used that way.

consist.etymology: From Middle French *consister*, from Latin *consistō* (“stand together, stop, become hard or solid, agree with, continue, exist”), from *com-* (“together”) + *sistō* (“to cause to stand, stand”).

senses.definition: A disease spread by contact.
The spread or transmission of such a disease.
The spread of anything likened to a contagious disease.
The passing on of manners or behavior through a closed community or household.

The spread of (initially small) shocks, which initially affect only a few financial institutions or a particular region of an economy, to other financial sectors and other countries whose economies were previously healthy.
A recession or crisis developed in such manner.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

core.definition: A disease that spreads from person to person, or the spread of a harmful idea or behavior through a group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the -TAY- syllable. The -gion ending sounds like juhn, with the g pronounced as a j, so do not say con-TAY-gee-on.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests danger and something that spreads out of control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contagion mostly in news, public health and literary writing, as in 'the contagion spread through the city.' In everyday speech people say 'the bug,' 'it's going around' or 'it's contagious.' Figuratively, contagion describes panic, rumors or trends that spread quickly, usually with a negative tone.

distinctions.note: An infection is an invasion of germs in one person; contagion stresses that the disease can spread from person to person.
An epidemic is a sudden rise in cases in one area; contagion describes the transmissible quality of the disease or idea.
A pandemic is a worldwide epidemic; contagion does not specify the scale.

examples.everyday: Stay home if you're sick so you don't spread the contagion to the office.
examples.professional: Our safety plan limits contagion by spacing out desks and asking sick staff to work from home.
examples.analytical: Sociologists often describe panic as a social contagion, in which fear spreads from person to person without any physical agent.

nuance.analogy: Contagion is like a wildfire: one spark can spread through dry grass until the whole field burns.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contagio, contact or touch, from contingere, to touch upon.
common_mistakes: Using contagion for a single sick person; it refers to the spread or the transmitted disease.
Confusing the noun contagion with the adjective contagious; say 'contagious' to describe something that spreads.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the -TAY- syllable.

contagion.etymology: From Middle English (late 14th century), from Old French, from Latin *contāgiō* (“a touching, contact, contagion”) related to *contingō* (“touch closely”).

senses.definition: Anything which cools.
An insulated bin or box used with ice or freezer packs to keep food or beverages cold while picnicking or camping.
A device for refrigerating dead bodies in a morgue.

Samalamig drink (sweet chilled beverage, such as chilled fruit juice or other flavors like chocolate, coffee, sweet corn, etc. usually mixed with either shredded jelly and/or sago pearls or tapioca pearls)
Ellipsis of air cooler, evaporative cooler, desert cooler, or swamp cooler.
A prison.
A bouncer or doorman.
A cold deck.
A loss suffered while holding a hand which is ordinarily strong, especially one which involves the loss of many chips.

core.definition: An insulated box filled with ice to keep food and drinks cold, especially for picnics, camping or beach trips.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final 'er' is a reduced, rhotic sound, so say it as 'ler' with the r pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical everyday word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, a cooler is the standard word for the portable insulated box people take on picnics, camping trips or beach days. It is often called an ice chest in some regions, especially in the South and Midwest. If you say 'ice box,' some older Americans may think of an old-fashioned refrigerator.

distinctions.note: Ice chest is a regional synonym, common in parts of the South and Midwest; cooler is the more widely understood term.
A refrigerator is a fixed appliance powered by electricity; a cooler is portable and uses ice or freezer packs.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the cooler from the trunk? The drinks are in it.
examples.professional: We'll need two coolers for the field trip, so please put the lunches on the ice before we leave.
examples.analytical: The cooler, as a device, reveals how modern leisure depends on the temporary control of temperature.

nuance.analogy: A cooler is a small, portable refrigerator with no plug, relying on ice to keep things cold.
nuance.etymology: Formed from cool and the suffix -er, meaning a thing that cools.
common_mistakes: Using cooler to mean a cool temperature; the adjective is cool, while cooler is the comparative or the noun for a box.
Saying 'cooler' for a refrigerator in a house; in American homes, refrigerator or fridge is the normal word.

conversation.text: Can you grab a soda for me from the cooler?
We packed a cooler with sandwiches, fruit, and drinks.
It's a little cooler by the water, so let's sit over there.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to correction; serving to correct.
senses.example: As the currents were changing rapidly, the captain had to make many corrective course changes.

senses.definition: Something that corrects or counteracts something.
senses.example: alkalies are correctives of acids

core.definition: Intended to fix, improve, or counteract something that is wrong or harmful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on REK. The -ive ending reduces to 'iv', not 'eeve'. Don't stress the first syllable, as in KOR-ek-tiv.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it implies improvement rather than punishment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use corrective in medicine (corrective lenses, corrective surgery), education, and the workplace (corrective action, corrective feedback). In everyday speech they say fix or make it right. Corrective is more formal and often describes measures or actions rather than people.

distinctions.note: Remedial means designed to remedy a deficiency, often in education; corrective is broader and more about fixing a particular error or condition.
Punitive means meant to punish; corrective is meant to fix or improve, not penalize.

examples.everyday: My eye doctor said I need corrective lenses for reading, not just glasses for distance.
examples.professional: We've taken corrective action on the server issue, so the outage shouldn't happen again.
examples.analytical: In Aristotle's account, corrective justice restores the balance disturbed by an unjust transaction.

nuance.analogy: Corrective is like a pair of glasses: they don't change the world, they adjust what you see so it becomes clear.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin correctivus, from Latin corrigere 'to correct'.
common_mistakes: Confusing corrective with correctional, which refers to prisons and jails.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying KOR-ek-tiv instead of kuh-REK-tiv.

senses.definition: To give off light; to reflect in flashes; to sparkle.
To exhibit brilliant technique or style.

core.definition: To flash or sparkle with bright, quick flashes of light.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, KAR-. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final syllable rhymes with 'mate.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests beauty, brilliance, or dazzling skill, usually in descriptive or literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use coruscate in speech; it appears in literary criticism, essays, and poetry, often for stars, jewels, or a brilliant speaker. A plain American speaker would say 'sparkle' or 'glitter' instead. Using it in casual talk can sound showy, so keep it for writing or formal praise.

distinctions.note: Sparkle is everyday and general; coruscate is literary and suggests more intense, brilliant flashes.
Glitter often implies showy surface shine; coruscate emphasizes repeated flashes of light, and sometimes of wit or skill.
Glimmer means faint, steady light; coruscate describes brighter, more dazzling flashes.

examples.everyday: The lake started to coruscate in the late sun, but my kids just wanted to jump in.
examples.professional: The keynote speaker's slides didn't coruscate, but her data story was clear and memorable.
examples.analytical: In his essays, the critic lets each paragraph coruscate with unexpected images that reward close reading.

nuance.analogy: To coruscate is like a diamond turned in sunlight: it throws off quick, bright flashes from many facets.
nuance.etymology: From Latin coruscare, 'to vibrate, glitter, flash.'
common_mistakes: Using coruscate in casual speech where sparkle is more natural.
Confusing coruscate with corrugate, a different verb meaning to form ridges.
Putting the stress on the second syllable, as kuh-RUS-kayt.

coruscate.etymology: From Latin *coruscātus*, perfect passive participle of *coruscō* (“to flash, gleam”), see *-ate*.

senses.definition: In a right triangle, the ratio of the length of the side adjacent to an acute angle to the length of the hypotenuse. Symbol: cos.

core.definition: In a right triangle, the ratio of the length of the side next to an acute angle to the length of the hypotenuse. Symbol: cos.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the first vowel as a long oh. The final 'sine' rhymes with 'line' and should not be pronounced with a separate 'e'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cosine in high school trigonometry, engineering, physics and data science. In speech people often say 'cos' or 'the cosine of theta' in formulas. The word is always neutral and technical, so no social register issues arise.

distinctions.note: Sine is the ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse, while cosine uses the adjacent side, so they are complementary in a right triangle.
Tangent is the ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent side, so it does not use the hypotenuse at all.

examples.everyday: My son's homework asked for the cosine of a forty-five degree angle, and I had to look it up.
examples.professional: We used cosine similarity to compare the embedding vectors, so documents with similar wording scored close to one.
examples.analytical: The law of cosines generalizes the Pythagorean theorem by adding a term that depends on the cosine of the included angle.

nuance.analogy: If the hypotenuse is a ladder leaning against a wall, the cosine tells you how far the foot of the ladder is from the wall, relative to the ladder's full length.
nuance.etymology: From Latin complementi sinus, meaning the sine of the complement, because cosine of an angle equals sine of its complement.
common_mistakes: Confusing cosine with sine, since both are ratios with the hypotenuse but use different sides.
Pronouncing the word with the stress on the second syllable.

cosine.etymology: From *co* + *sine*, short for *complementi sinus* in Latin, meaning “sine of the complement”.

senses.definition: The study of the physical universe, its structure, dynamics, origin and evolution, and fate.
A metaphysical study into the origin and nature of the universe.
A particular view (cultural or religious) of the structure and origin of the universe.

core.definition: The scientific and philosophical study of the universe's origin, structure, evolution and eventual fate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'MAH', and the final syllable is 'jee'. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'luh-juh'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American universities, cosmology is a branch of astronomy and physics, and cosmologists study the Big Bang and dark energy. The word can also refer to a culture's view of the universe, as in 'Mayan cosmology'. Use it neutrally in academic and everyday talk about science.

distinctions.note: Astronomy studies celestial objects such as stars and planets, while cosmology studies the universe as a whole, including its origin and large-scale structure.
Cosmogony is specifically about the origin of the universe, while cosmology covers its structure, evolution and fate as well.

examples.everyday: My brother got really into cosmology after watching documentaries about black holes and the Big Bang.
examples.professional: Our research group uses large simulation datasets to test models in observational cosmology.
examples.analytical: A theological cosmology must explain how creation depends on God while still making sense of the scientific account of the universe's history.

nuance.analogy: If astronomy is a field guide to individual birds, cosmology is the study of the entire ecosystem and how it began and changes over time.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kosmos, meaning order or world, plus logia, meaning study.
common_mistakes: Confusing cosmology with cosmetology, the study of beauty treatments.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'KAHZ-muh-lah-jee'.

cosmology.etymology: From Medieval Latin *cosmologia*, from Ancient Greek *κόσμος* (“world”) + *-λογία* (“treating of”), combination form of *-λόγος* (“one who speaks”).

senses.definition: Sad because of a disappointment.

core.definition: Sad and disappointed, especially after failing at something or hearing bad news.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KREST. The second syllable 'fall' has the aw vowel, and the final syllable is a reduced schwa followed by n.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes sadness and loss of confidence after disappointment, often with a sympathetic tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'crestfallen' to describe someone who looks visibly disappointed, such as a child who lost a game or a candidate who did not win. It is more common in writing and storytelling than in casual talk, where people often say 'bummed' or 'really disappointed.' It sounds slightly expressive and warm, not harsh.

distinctions.note: Sad is a general word for unhappiness, while crestfallen specifically describes disappointment that shows in one's posture or face.
Disappointed is the everyday, neutral term, while crestfallen is more vivid and suggests visible dejection.

examples.everyday: He looked crestfallen when he got home, because he had not made the team.
examples.professional: After the client rejected our proposal, the crestfallen team spent the afternoon reviewing what went wrong.
examples.analytical: The character's crestfallen silence reveals a deeper disappointment in his own ideals rather than only in the outcome.

nuance.analogy: Crestfallen is like a rooster whose comb has drooped: the pride that stood up straight has collapsed.
nuance.etymology: From crest, the top of a bird's head, and fallen, from the image of a drooping comb after defeat.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'crest-fallen' with a hyphen in careful writing; the standard spelling is one word, 'crestfallen.'
Using it for anger; it describes disappointment and sadness, not frustration.

crestfallen.etymology: From *crest* + *fallen*, from the appearance of a horse with its crest on its chest after defeat in a battle.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to the complex roots of unity.
Of, or relating to cyclotomy.

core.definition: Relating to the complex roots of unity, or to the division of a circle into equal parts in number theory.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TAH, the third syllable. Americans pronounce the 'o' in the middle of 'cyclo' as a long 'oh', and the final syllable is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized mathematical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Only mathematicians and advanced students use this word, typically in number theory and algebra. Americans would rarely use it in conversation, and a general audience would not understand it without explanation. In a graduate seminar or a paper, it is the correct term.

distinctions.note: Cyclic means repeating or circular in general, while cyclotomic is a precise term about roots of unity and dividing a circle.
Circular refers to a round shape in everyday speech, while cyclotomic is a technical term from algebra and geometry.

examples.everyday: My son's math homework used the word cyclotomic, and I had to look it up.
examples.professional: Our cryptography team studied cyclotomic fields because they simplify certain modular calculations.
examples.analytical: The cyclotomic polynomial of order n has as its roots exactly the primitive nth roots of unity.

nuance.analogy: A cyclotomic polynomial is like a set of evenly spaced markers around a clock face, each one a distinct point on the circle.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kyklos, 'circle', and tomē, 'cutting', via cyclotomy, the division of a circle.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'sy-kloh-TOH-mik'; the stress belongs on the 'tah' syllable.
Using it as a general synonym for 'cyclic' or 'circular' in ordinary speech.

senses.definition: To make slightly wet or soiled by spattering or sprinkling a liquid (such as water, mud, or paint) on it; to bedabble.
To cause splashing by moving a body part like a bill or limb in soft mud, water, etc. often playfully; to play in shallow water; to paddle.
senses.example: The children sat on the dock and dabbled their feet in the water.

senses.definition: To feed without diving, by submerging the head and neck underwater to seek food, often also tipping up the tail straight upwards above the water.
To participate or have an interest in an activity in a casual or superficial way.
senses.example: She’s an actress by trade, but has been known to dabble in poetry.

senses.definition: A spattering or sprinkling of a liquid.
An act of splashing in soft mud, water, etc.
An act of participation in an activity in a casual or superficial way.

core.definition: To take part in an activity casually or without serious commitment, or to splash lightly in water or mud.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a light 'l' with a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'DAB-uhl.' Do not add an extra vowel between 'b' and 'l.'

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or neutral; it suggests a casual, shallow involvement rather than serious work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dabble to describe trying an interest or skill without going deep, such as dabbling in painting or cooking. It sounds friendly and modest, and it can be a polite way to say you are not an expert. People might say they 'dabble in the stock market' to signal small, casual investments. Avoid using it for serious professional work, where it can sound dismissive.

distinctions.note: Dabble implies casual, light participation, while 'study' or 'work' imply serious, sustained commitment.
Tinker suggests making small adjustments to improve something, while dabble suggests trying something out without depth.

examples.everyday: I dabble in gardening on weekends, but I still buy most of my vegetables at the farmers market.
examples.professional: Our team dabbles in machine learning, but the core product still relies on traditional statistical models.
examples.analytical: Philosophers who only dabble in ethics often miss the deep tensions that specialists have spent decades analyzing.

nuance.analogy: To dabble is like dipping one toe into a lake before deciding whether to swim.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English dabelen, a frequentative of dabben, to splash.
common_mistakes: Using 'dabble on' instead of 'dabble in' with an activity.
Pronouncing it 'DAB-ble' with a clearly pronounced extra vowel.

senses.definition: A non-clerical role for women in some churches.
A female deacon.
A female servant in the early Christian church.
The nun in charge of the altar in a convent.
One of an order of women in some Protestant churches who nurse the sick and tend the poor.

core.definition: A woman who serves in a church in a ministry of service and charity, sometimes formally commissioned or ordained, depending on the denomination.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the last syllable, 'NESS,' with a secondary stress on 'dee.' Do not put the stress on 'dee' as in 'deacon.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; evokes service, though some find the term dated where women serve as deacons.
nuance.usage_note: Some churches, such as Lutheran and Methodist ones, have formal deaconess orders. Many churches now simply say 'deacon' for both men and women. Choose the term the particular church uses.

distinctions.note: Deacon is the general office; deaconess specifically marks a woman and may denote a distinct, non-clergy role.
A nun belongs to a religious order under vows, while a deaconess serves in the church without necessarily taking monastic vows.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was a deaconess and visited sick members every week.
examples.professional: The seminary offers a program that prepares students for ministry as pastors or deaconesses.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether Phoebe in Romans 16 held a formal office or served informally as a deaconess.

nuance.etymology: From deacon plus the feminine suffix -ess, from Late Latin diaconissa.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'DEE-kuh-ness'; stress the last syllable.
Assuming it always means an ordained clergy member; it often does not.
nuance.biblical_note: Romans 16:1 calls Phoebe a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae; the RSV renders it 'deaconess,' while the Greek word is the same as for male deacons. 1 Timothy 3:11 mentions 'women' (or deacons' wives) in the context of deacon qualifications, and translators differ on its meaning.

traditions.view: The early church had ordained deaconesses who assisted with women's baptism and care; the order is not widely active today, though some call for its revival.
Women deacons existed in the early church, but today the diaconate is limited to men. The question of women deacons has been studied by commissions.
Practice differs: Lutheran deaconess communities exist, Methodist and Anglican churches may ordain or consecrate women as deacons, and many Baptist churches have women deacons or none.

senses.definition: A person or object meant to lure somebody into danger.
A real or fake animal used by hunters to lure game.
Deceptive military device used to draw enemy attention or fire away from a more important target.
An assembly of hooped or netted corridors into which wild ducks may be enticed (originally by tame ducks) and trapped.
To lead into danger by artifice; to lure into a net or snare; to entrap.
senses.example: to decoy troops into an ambush; to decoy ducks into a net

senses.definition: To act as, or use, a decoy.
senses.example: As they were being decoyed, the rescue team carried the hostage and quietly slipped away.

core.definition: A person or object used to trick or lure someone or something into a trap, danger, or wrong position.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable in the noun. As a verb, Americans stress the second syllable: 'dih-KOY'. The item's schwa-initial form is the verb pattern, so use the stress shift for the noun.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral; it implies deception, though a decoy may be used for protection or sport.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'decoy' for hunting decoys, police or military tactics, and figurative talk about a distraction. Phrases like 'decoy car' or 'be a decoy' are common in news and movies. In casual talk, saying someone 'was used as a decoy' implies they were deliberately used to draw attention.

distinctions.note: 'Bait' is food or a lure used to catch something; 'decoy' is a fake or misleading object or person that imitates a target.
A 'distraction' simply diverts attention, while a 'decoy' is deliberately designed to lure into danger or away from a target.

examples.everyday: The hunter set up a wooden duck decoy near the pond to attract the birds.
examples.professional: Our security team used a decoy account to see whether the phishing emails would reach the real staff.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the tempting promise as a decoy, leading the reader away from the deeper question of what makes life meaningful.

nuance.analogy: A decoy is like a fake cake left on a table to tempt a thief away from the real treasure.
nuance.etymology: From Dutch de kooi, 'the decoy cage', from Latin cavea, 'cage'.
common_mistakes: Using the verb pronunciation for the noun; the noun stresses the first syllable.
Confusing 'decoy' with 'bait', which is used to catch something directly.

senses.definition: In a defensible manner.
Defendably.

core.definition: In a way that can be justified or reasonably defended.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of the stem, FEN. The final -ly is a clear 'lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a choice or claim is reasonable, though not necessarily perfect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use defensibly in formal writing, reviews, and analysis to say something can be reasonably justified. It is rare in casual speech; in conversation people usually say 'reasonably' or 'you can make a case for it'. Avoid the nonstandard 'defendably' in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Reasonably is the everyday choice; defensibly is more formal and implies the position would survive criticism.
Justifiably stresses that good grounds exist; defensibly stresses that the position can be held against objections.

examples.everyday: You could defensibly say the restaurant was overpriced, but the food was good.
examples.professional: We can defensibly exclude those outliers, since they come from a broken sensor.
examples.analytical: The author defensibly argues that moral intuitions carry evidential weight, even if they cannot be fully systematized.

nuance.analogy: Like a fence built on solid posts: it stands up to a push because the structure is sound.
nuance.etymology: From defensible, from defend, from Latin defendere, plus -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'defendably', which is nonstandard in formal American English.
Using it in casual speech where 'reasonably' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Great respect.
senses.example: The children treated their elders with deference.

senses.definition: The willingness to carry out the wishes of others.
senses.example: By tidying his room, he showed deference to his mother.

core.definition: Polite respect for someone's wishes, authority, or expertise, often shown by yielding to them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DEF. The middle syllable is reduced to 'er', and the final -ence is 'uns'.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it shows respect, but it can sound negative if it implies excessive submission.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deference in discussions of hierarchy, expertise, and manners: 'out of deference to her seniority'. In casual speech they often say 'respect' instead. 'Deference' suggests the respect involves yielding to someone's judgment, so it can sound stiff in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Respect is broader and everyday; deference specifically means yielding to another's wishes or authority.
Obedience means following orders; deference is a voluntary yielding out of respect and does not always involve following commands.

examples.everyday: Out of deference to my grandmother, we waited until she sat down before we started eating.
examples.professional: Out of deference to the senior engineers, I held my proposal until they had reviewed the architecture.
examples.analytical: Weber distinguishes legitimate authority from mere habits of deference, asking why people accept rule at all.

nuance.analogy: Like stepping aside at a doorway to let someone pass: the gesture acknowledges their claim to go first.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin deferentia, from Latin deferre 'to bring down, submit, yield'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'DEE-fer-ence'; the stress is on the first syllable, DEF.
Using 'deference' for 'difference' or 'defiance' by mistake; check the spelling.

core.definition: A personal name in the Hebrew Bible, borne by several men, including a secretary of King Jehoiakim who opposed the burning of Jeremiah's scroll.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LAY, and end with a light 'uh'. The name has three syllables, not two.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical name with no everyday sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Delaiah mainly in Bible study, in sermons, or in reference works about biblical names. It is not used in ordinary conversation. Someone might simply say Oh, I remember Delaiah from Jeremiah if the topic comes up.

distinctions.note: The name is shared by several different men in the Bible, so the passage determines which Delaiah is meant.

examples.everyday: Do you remember who Delaiah was in the story of the scroll?
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, Delaiah appears as one of the officials who urged the king to spare the scroll.
examples.analytical: The text names Delaiah among the officials who resisted the king's command, which marks him as a moral contrast to the king.

nuance.analogy: Delaiah is like a name on a roll call: it identifies a particular person by reference to a specific moment in the story.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Delayahu, meaning 'Yahweh has drawn out' or 'Yahweh has set free'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as DEL-ay-uh, stressing the first syllable.
Confusing it with Delilah, a different biblical name.
nuance.biblical_note: Delaiah (Hebrew Delayahu, 'Yahweh has drawn out' or 'Yahweh has set free') is the name of several men. In Jeremiah 36:12 and 36:25 Delaiah son of Shemaiah is an official who objects when King Jehoiakim orders Jeremiah's scroll to be burned. In Ezra 2:60 and Nehemiah 7:62, the sons of Delaiah are listed among those who returned from exile in Babylon.

senses.definition: Asking whether someone saw something online.

core.definition: Asking whether someone has watched a particular video, often one shared online or on a phone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of 'video' (VIH-dee-oh), and in fast speech 'did you' sounds like 'dih-JOO'. Say 'that' with a short a, as in 'hat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is casual and invites a shared reaction, though it can feel pushy if repeated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this at work, with friends, or with family after someone shares a clip on a phone. It is casual and expects a quick reply, such as 'Yes, that was hilarious!' or 'No, send it to me.' Saying 'Did you see that video?' about a long or disturbing clip may need more context.
